'''Paco1994''' is the working name for a not-yet-implemented ScummVM engine targeting '''''Paco El Hare vs Los Marcianos Siderales''''' ("Paco the Hare vs. the Sidereal Martians"), a 1994 Spanish MS-DOS freeware title by '''Alcachofa Soft S.L.''' — the same studio later responsible for ''[[Drascula: The Vampire Strikes Back]]''. The 1994 title is a small, unfinished point-and-click adventure tech demo, not a commercial release. This page documents the complete reverse-engineering of its file formats and runtime behavior, undertaken to evaluate and prepare its addition to ScummVM.

__TOC__

== Overview ==

''Paco El Hare vs Los Marcianos Siderales'' is a 320×200, 256-color VGA Mode 13h point-and-click adventure running natively under MS-DOS Real Mode (x86 16-bit). It was distributed as freeware, apparently as a conceptual prototype or vertical-slice demo rather than a finished commercial product: the available distribution contains only 5 of an implied 11+ scenes, and several referenced assets (a shared sprite sheet, some scene backgrounds, some dialogue audio, and all background music files) are absent from every known copy of the release.

The engine is architecturally '''hybrid''': room geometry, hotspot rectangles, door connectivity, and sprite placement are '''data-driven''', read at runtime from small per-scene <code>.ALD</code> text files. Dialogue text, puzzle logic, and item-interaction rules are '''hardcoded''' as C <code>if</code>/<code>switch</code> chains compiled directly into the main executable, <code>HARE.EXE</code>. There is no bytecode, no script interpreter, and no external narrative script file of any kind — a point worth stating plainly because it is easy to over-read the presence of a data file format as evidence of a full scripting system, which this engine does not have.

== Legal status ==

The game's title screen carries no explicit license text beyond an implied "freeware" distribution; no separate license file has been found in any known copy. Under Spanish and EU intellectual-property law, informal "freeware" distribution does not by itself grant modification, redistribution, or reverse-engineering-for-competition rights — it grants permission to use the software at no cost, nothing more.

'''Major update: this game has a legitimate, current, free official re-release.''' As of February 2, 2024, ''Paco El Hare vs Los Marcianos Siderales'' is distributed for free on Steam (App ID 1643000), with '''Alcachofa Soft''' credited as developer and '''Erbe Software''' credited as publisher — confirmed directly from the official Steam store listing, not a third-party aggregator. The store description explicitly frames it as this same 1994 demo, historically significant as "the first development by Alcachofa Soft," originally pitched to Dinamic Multimedia, whose technology and concept directly fed into the creation of ''Drascula: The Vampire Strikes Back''. This is not a remake or a completed sequel; it is the same unfinished tech demo, formally re-released.

'''Erbe Software, S.L.''' is a real, currently-operating, registered Spanish company (CIF B76782309, Registro Mercantil de Santa Cruz de Tenerife, tomo 3597, folio 42, hoja TF-61859), directed by '''Marcos García de la Rosa''', founded in late 2018 and independent since the end of 2024. Their published catalog (confirmed via their own itch.io storefront) includes multiple '''other''' Alcachofa Soft titles under active republication — ''Drascula: The Vampire Strikes Back'' and ''The Abbey — Director's Cut'' among them — indicating an ongoing, multi-title publishing relationship with the Alcachofa Soft catalog, not a one-off arrangement specific to this game. Erbe Software also republishes the Mortadelo y Filemón game series digitally — the exact same license family targeted by the '''existing, unrelated''' ScummVM <code>alcachofa</code> engine described under [[#Relationship to the existing Alcachofa engine|Relationship to the existing Alcachofa engine]] below. A single modern rights-holder therefore sits behind both that existing engine's source material and this article's subject, which is a materially useful fact for any future contact: '''proyectos@erbesoftware.com''' is Erbe Software's own listed address specifically for external parties proposing collaborative publishing/preservation work, alongside general (contacto@) and press (prensa@) addresses.

'''Provenance of the analysis in this article:''' the complete original file set examined here — including the six previously-unavailable scenes, the sprite sheet, all five music files, and the voice driver — was sourced from a DOSBox-ready preservation package whose included shortcut file resolves to <code>https://www.abandonsocios.org/wiki/Paco_el_Hare_vs_los_Marcianos_Siderales</code>, a page on AbandonSocios ("the portal of old games"), a longstanding Spanish abandonware/retro-gaming preservation community. The package's own bundled <code>dosbox.conf</code> credits its assembly to a community packager using the handle "cireja," dated February 2026, and specifies the actual settings used to run the game correctly: <code>machine=svga_s3</code>, <code>sbtype=sb16</code>, <code>sbbase=220</code>, <code>irq=7</code>, <code>dma=1</code>, <code>oplmode=auto</code>, <code>oplrate=44100</code>, <code>cycles=2000</code> — this is real, verified configuration data superseding the estimated <code>cycles=fixed 4000</code> suggestion in an earlier revision of this article's [[#Game loop and timing|Game loop and timing]] section. The package's <code>autoexec</code> sequence confirms <code>SBFMDRV.COM</code> is launched before <code>HARE.EXE</code>, exactly as this article's [[#SBFMDRV.COM|SBFMDRV.COM]] section already documented from binary analysis alone.

Recommended request, in order of preference, updated in light of the above:
# Contact Erbe Software directly (<code>proyectos@erbesoftware.com</code>) referencing both their existing Steam distribution of this exact title and their established Alcachofa Soft/Drascula relationship with ScummVM — this is now a substantially stronger position than reaching for a defunct 1994 studio with no findable modern contact, since a real, active, rights-holding publisher is already distributing this precise game for free.
# In parallel, the original Drascula precedent remains valid and complementary: in August 2008, '''Emilio de Paz Aragón''' of Alcachofa Soft personally provided ScummVM with the full source code of ''Drascula: The Vampire Strikes Back'' and re-released that game as freeware; he is credited by name on the official [https://www.scummvm.org/credits/ ScummVM Credits page] for doing so.
# Failing a response from either, treatment under ScummVM's standard policy for engines built via clean-room reverse engineering without vendor source (see [[Engines/ScummVM Engine HowTo]]): this is the path already taken for this analysis, and is why a complete, working reference implementation (see [[#ScummVM implementation|below]]) was produced before any code was proposed for inclusion — per ScummVM's own stated position, reverse-engineering a game without source is accepted, but only as serious, substantial work backed by a developer willing to see it through, not a request made on spec.

Any eventual "community completion" or extension of the game beyond its original scope would constitute a derivative work and should be presented to Erbe Software as a clearly-labeled fan project, not a claimed original release — this is a materially easier conversation to have now that a real publisher contact exists, rather than none at all.

== Technical architecture ==

=== Toolchain identification ===

Both primary executables are conclusively identified as '''Borland Turbo C 2.0''' output via multiple independent signals:

{| class="wikitable"
! Evidence !! Detail
|-
| Borland TDS debug symbols || Magic bytes <code>0xFB 0x52</code>, version <code>0x0208</code>, appended after the MZ image in both <code>HARE.EXE</code> and <code>SCOVA.EXE</code>. Symbol count is sensitive to tokenization method — see note below.
|-
| CRT copyright string || Literal string <code>"Turbo-C - Copyright (c) 1988 Borland Intl."</code> present verbatim in both binaries' data segments
|-
| CRT symbol <code>__turboCrt</code> || Present only in Borland Turbo C/C++ output; absent from Microsoft C and Watcom builds
|-
| Entry-point opcode pattern || <code>BA ?? ?? 2E 89 16 ?? ??</code> (<code>MOV DX,&lt;dseg_size&gt;; CS: MOV [off],DX</code>) — the standard Borland TLINK startup sequence
|-
| Relocation density || 87 entries (<code>HARE.EXE</code>) and 101 entries (<code>SCOVA.EXE</code>), consistent with Borland TLINK medium/large-model output using far pointers
|}

{{Note|'''On symbol counts:''' the exact number of unique TDS symbols reported for this binary has varied across analysis passes (351, then 398 in a secondary source, now 348 here) because naive substring scanning of the raw TDS bytes can slice a token mid-identifier (e.g. extracting <code>_BPsafe</code> out of the middle of an unrelated longer string) and inflate the count. A boundary-safe re-extraction — requiring every candidate token to begin immediately after a non-identifier byte — yields '''348 unique symbols in <code>HARE.EXE</code>''' and '''347 in <code>SCOVA.EXE</code>''', with 328 shared between the two and the remainder split between EMS-only symbols in <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> and a small number of <code>HARE.EXE</code>-only symbols. This is the count used throughout this article.}}

<code>PLAY.EXE</code> and <code>VPLAY.EXE</code> are a separate toolchain entirely: both carry the string <code>"MS Run-Time Library - Copyright (c) 1987, Microsoft Corp"</code> and have zero relocation entries (position-independent code), identifying them as Microsoft C output.

==== Instruction-level confirmation: CRT startup signatures ====

Every piece of toolchain evidence above is either a string (which could in principle be altered without affecting behavior) or a structural header field. The strongest possible confirmation is at the instruction level: manually disassembling each executable's actual entry-point bytes and comparing the two toolchains' startup '''conventions''', not just their self-reported banners. All four bytes sequences below were extracted directly from each file's own MZ-header-computed entry point (<code>header_size + CS×16 + IP</code>) and hand-disassembled.

'''<code>HARE.EXE</code> / <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> entry point (identical pattern in both):'''
<syntaxhighlight lang="asm">
BA AA 0B          MOV  DX, 0x0BAA        ; data segment size, in paragraphs
2E 89 16 BA 01    MOV  CS:[0x01BA], DX   ; store it — the Borland-specific
                                          ; "save data segment size" idiom
B4 30             MOV  AH, 0x30          ; DOS function 0x30
CD 21             INT  0x21              ; = "Get MS-DOS Version Number"
8B 2E 02 00       MOV  BP, [0x0002]      ; PSP+0x02: top of allocated memory
8B 1E 2C 00       MOV  BX, [0x002C]      ; PSP+0x2C: environment block segment
8E DA             MOV  DS, DX
A3 7D 00          MOV  [0x007D], AX
8C 06 7B 00       MOV  [0x007B], ES
89 1E 77 ..       MOV  [0x0077], BX      ; (truncated)
</syntaxhighlight>
Querying the DOS version via <code>INT 21h AH=30h</code> as the '''second''' executed operation (immediately after the data-segment-size save), followed by reading the allocated-memory and environment-segment fields directly out of the Program Segment Prefix at fixed offsets 0x02 and 0x2C, is the textbook Borland Turbo C small-model-family CRT startup (the <code>C0*.OBJ</code> family, here specifically <code>C0C.OBJ</code> — see the confirmed Compact-model finding below). This sequence differs from Microsoft C's own startup at essentially every instruction.

'''<code>PLAY.EXE</code> / <code>VPLAY.EXE</code> entry point (identical pattern in both, and different from the above at every instruction):'''
<syntaxhighlight lang="asm">
8C C0             MOV  AX, ES
05 10 00          ADD  AX, 0x0010
0E                PUSH CS
1F                POP  DS
A3 04 00          MOV  [0x0004], AX
03 06 0C 00       ADD  AX, [0x000C]
8E C0             MOV  ES, AX
8B 0E 06 00       MOV  CX, [0x0006]
8B F9             MOV  DI, CX
4F                DEC  DI
8B F7             MOV  SI, DI
FD                STD                    ; set direction flag — copy will run backward
F3 A4             REP  MOVSB             ; reverse block copy, CX bytes
8B 16 0E 00       MOV  DX, [0x000E]
</syntaxhighlight>
Computing an adjusted segment (<code>ES = CS + 0x10 + [0x000C]</code>) and then performing a '''reverse''' (<code>STD</code>-then-<code>REP MOVSB</code>) block copy to compact/relocate the program image is the classic Microsoft C small-model <code>.EXE</code> startup convention — categorically different from Borland's DOS-version-check-first pattern above. This confirms, at the level of actual executed machine code rather than an embedded string that could in principle be edited or forged, that <code>PLAY.EXE</code>/<code>VPLAY.EXE</code> were built by a genuinely different compiler and linker than <code>HARE.EXE</code>/<code>SCOVA.EXE</code> — the strongest form of toolchain evidence available short of the original source.

=== Binary structural layout ===

Coarse layout of <code>HARE.EXE</code>, reconstructed from MZ header fields, the confirmed TDS trailer position, and string-cluster locations. The TDS symbol table position below is not an estimate — it is the exact computed boundary between the MZ image and the post-image data, verified to the byte against the header's own page-count fields.

{| class="wikitable"
! File offset !! Approx. size !! Content
|-
| 0x00000 || 512 B || MZ header (32-paragraph header, per the header's own <code>header_para</code> field) plus relocation table
|-
| 0x00200 || — || Entry point / CRT0 startup (Borland Turbo C 2.0 initialization stub)
|-
| ~0x00500–0x0BE00 || ~46 KB || Code and initialized data: video/audio/mouse init, sprite blitter, input handlers, CRT library code, scene rendering, sound and dialogue handlers (boundaries between these regions were not individually delimited; this range is the code+data body between CRT0 and the string cluster below)
|-
| ~0x0BE00–0x0E4A6 || ~9.9 KB || Data segment string cluster: embedded filenames, dialogue text, error messages (see [[#Embedded strings and file references|Embedded strings and file references]])
|-
| 0x0E4A6 || 22,645 B || Post-image data: Borland TDS v2.08 symbol table (magic <code>0xFB52</code>) and TDS unit/module name list. '''This offset is exact''': it equals <code>(pages−1)×512 + last_page_bytes</code> computed from the MZ header, and independently equals the file offset at which the <code>0xFB 0x52</code> TDS magic actually occurs — the two derivations agree to the byte.
|}

=== MZ header summary ===

{| class="wikitable"
! Field !! HARE.EXE !! SCOVA.EXE !! PLAY.EXE !! VPLAY.EXE
|-
| File size || 81,179 B || 77,863 B || 37,739 B || 20,893 B
|-
| MZ image size || 58,534 B || 56,134 B || 37,739 B || 20,893 B
|-
| Post-image data || 22,645 B (Borland TDS) || 21,729 B (Borland TDS) || 0 B || 0 B
|-
| Relocation entries || 87 || 101 || 0 || 0
|-
| Entry point (file offset) || 0x000200 || 0x000200 || 0x008E62 || 0x005032
|-

<code>HARE.EXE</code> and <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> differ in exactly one meaningful way at the entry point: <code>HARE.EXE</code> reserves a 0x0BAA-paragraph data segment where <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> reserves 0x0B0D — a 2,512-byte difference, consistent with <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> moving some string data out of the conventional-memory data segment to make room for its EMS usage (see below).

=== Memory model ===

<code>HARE.EXE</code> runs entirely within 640 KB conventional memory. <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> additionally requires 256 KB of LIM EMS 4.0 expanded memory (confirmed via TDS symbols <code>_ems_alloc</code>, <code>_ems_map</code>, <code>_ems_free</code>, <code>_ems_frame_seg</code>, <code>_ems_version</code>, and the literal error string <code>"Este programa necesita 256 Kb de memoria EMS para funcionar."</code>). The EMS page frame provides four 16 KB physical window slots mapped from a 16-logical-page (256 KB) allocation; typical frame segment values are 0xD000 or 0xE000 depending on the host BIOS.

Key conventional-memory regions relevant to a from-scratch engine implementation:

{| class="wikitable"
! Region !! Purpose
|-
| 0x00000–0x004FF || IVT + BIOS Data Area
|-
| 0x00800–~0x1FFFF || DOS kernel, COMMAND.COM, TSRs (SBFMDRV.COM loads here)
|-
| CS:0000 onward || <code>HARE.EXE</code> code + data image (58.5 KB)
|-
| Far heap (farmalloc pool) || 64000-byte ALG background buffer, 64000-byte back-buffer, preloaded VOC buffers (<code>_dir_voc_s1/s2/s3</code>), <code>ct-voice.drv</code> image
|-
| 0xA0000–0xAFFFF || VGA VRAM, Mode 13h active window (destination of the per-frame page flip)
|-
| 0xD0000/0xE0000 region || EMS page frame (<code>SCOVA.EXE</code> only)
|}

=== Rendering pipeline ===

Video is initialized with <code>INT 10h, AH=00h, AL=13h</code> (Mode 13h: 320×200, 256 colors, linear framebuffer at segment <code>A000</code>). The palette DAC is programmed through ports <code>0x3C8</code> (index) and <code>0x3C9</code> (RGB triplet, ×3 writes per index); the DAC accepts only 6-bit values (0–63) per channel, so an 8-bit source palette (as found in the game's PCX assets) must be right-shifted by 2 before being written to hardware — this shift is '''not''' needed when targeting a modern 8-bit <code>Graphics::Surface</code>, only when emulating the literal hardware path.

Per-frame layer composition, reconstructed from the TDS symbol table and cross-referenced against the game's own asset structure:

{| class="wikitable"
! Layer !! Symbol !! Operation
|-
| 0 || <code>_borra_pantalla</code> || Clear 64000-byte back-buffer to palette index 0
|-
| 1 || <code>_pon_dibujos</code> || Blit decoded background (64000-byte copy from the far-heap ALG buffer)
|-
| 2 || <code>_pon_dibujos_colocao</code> || Blit disc-object sprites (from the missing <code>99.ALG</code> sheet) at ALD-specified coordinates, masked
|-
| 3 || <code>_pon_hare</code> || Blit the player-character sprite via <code>_DIBUJA_BLOQUE_CON_MASK</code>
|-
| 4 || <code>_pon_dibujos_menu</code> / <code>menu_sin_volcar</code> || Inventory HUD overlay, no page flip yet
|-
| 5 || (part of <code>_hablar</code>) || Dialogue box: black rectangle at rows 155–199, centered text via <code>_centra_texto</code>
|-
| FLIP || <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA</code> || <code>REP MOVSW</code>, 32,000 words, back-buffer → <code>A000:0000</code>
|}

Sprite compositing uses <code>_DIBUJA_BLOQUE_CON_MASK</code>: destination = (destination AND mask) OR (source AND NOT mask), i.e. a standard AND/OR masked blit with a separate 1-bit-per-pixel-equivalent mask plane rather than a single transparent color key.

==== Masked blit — reference implementation ====

The mask plane in this engine is stored at the '''same bit depth as the sprite''' (a full 8-bit-per-pixel companion bitmap, not a packed 1-bit-per-pixel plane) — this follows directly from the confirmed <code>99.ALG</code> sprite-sheet layout, where each sprite row has a corresponding mask row offset +56 pixels below it in the '''same PCX file''' (see [[#99.ALG — shared sprite sheet (now obtained; geometry solved and verified against real pixels)|99.ALG]]), rather than a separate, differently-encoded mask resource. A mask pixel value of <code>0x00</code> means "fully transparent, show the background," any other value means "fully opaque, show the sprite" — there is no partial/alpha blending in a 256-color indexed engine of this era. '''Update:''' now that the real sheet has been obtained, the mask rows do not show a clean uniform black/white transparency pattern — see the open note under [[#99.ALG — shared sprite sheet (now obtained; geometry solved and verified against real pixels)|99.ALG]] for what remains unresolved about exactly how these mask pixels are used.

<syntaxhighlight lang="c">
// dst:  destination back-buffer, DST_STRIDE bytes per row (320 for the full back-buffer)
// src:  source sprite pixels, sprite_w x sprite_h, tightly packed (sprite_w bytes/row)
// mask: source mask pixels, same dimensions and packing as src
// dx,dy: destination top-left in the back-buffer
void dibuja_bloque_con_mask(uint8_t *dst, int dst_stride,
                             const uint8_t *src, const uint8_t *mask,
                             int sprite_w, int sprite_h,
                             int dx, int dy) {
    for (int y = 0; y < sprite_h; y++) {
        uint8_t *drow = dst + (dy + y) * dst_stride + dx;
        const uint8_t *srow = src  + y * sprite_w;
        const uint8_t *mrow = mask + y * sprite_w;
        for (int x = 0; x < sprite_w; x++) {
            if (mrow[x] != 0x00)          // opaque: mask byte non-zero
                drow[x] = srow[x];
            // mask byte == 0x00: transparent, leave destination pixel untouched
        }
    }
}

// _DIBUJA_BLOQUE_CON_MASK_CUT is the same operation with (dx,dy,sprite_w,sprite_h)
// pre-clipped against the 320x200 back-buffer bounds before the loop above runs,
// for sprites that straddle a screen edge (e.g. a hotspot near x=0 or x=319).

// _DIBUJA_BLOQUE_SIN_MASK is the unconditional case (background fill, full-screen
// PCX blit): drop the "if (mrow[x] != 0)" test and always assign drow[x] = srow[x].
</syntaxhighlight>

==== Page flip — corrected: _VUELCA_PANTALLA is an 8-parameter partial-blit function ====

{{Note|'''Major correction.''' This article previously described <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA</code> as a fixed-size, argument-free, unconditional 64,000-byte copy with "no dirty-rectangle tracking of any kind." Direct comparison of the real <code>HARE.EXE</code> Reko decompilation against a secondary source's claim shows this was wrong. The correction and its evidence are given in full below, since the earlier claim was stated with more confidence than the underlying disassembly actually supported.}}

The real Reko-decompiled signature, confirmed against roughly fifty independent call sites in <code>HARE.EXE</code>, is:

<syntaxhighlight lang="c">
void _VUELCA_PANTALLA(word16 dest_x, word16 dest_y, word16 src_x, word16 src_y,
                       word16 width, word16 height, selector seg, word16 offset);
</syntaxhighlight>

'''Eight parameters, not zero.''' Every observed call site has <code>dest_x == src_x</code> and <code>dest_y == src_y</code> — the function is called to copy a rectangle from a position in the named far buffer to the '''same''' position on the physical screen, never to reposition content. Two representative confirmed call shapes:

{| class="wikitable"
! Call !! Meaning
|-
| <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA(0, 0, 0, 0, 0x140, 200, backbuf_seg, backbuf_off)</code> || Full-screen refresh: (0,0), 320×200 (<code>0x140</code> = 320) — the whole-frame case
|-
| <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA(0x3E, 0x5E, 0x3E, 0x5E, 0x35, 0x28, seg, off)</code> || A small 53×40 region at (62, 94) — this exact position matches the slot-machine's red button (see [[#Cross-verification log|Cross-verification log]] for the source and verification of this coordinate)
|}

This means the engine '''does''' support partial/rectangular screen updates through this single general-purpose primitive — the earlier "no dirty-rectangle tracking of any kind" claim in this article was incorrect; it is more precise to say that no '''automatic''' dirty-tracking exists (nothing computes which regions changed on its own), but the engine's own code deliberately invokes small-rectangle updates in specific situations, such as redrawing a slot-machine button, rather than paying for a full 64,000-byte transfer for a 53×40-pixel change.

'''Reconciling this with the assembly this article previously presented as <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA</code>'s own body:''' the fixed, argument-free 32,000-word <code>REP MOVSW</code> sequence shown in an earlier revision of this section is very likely real machine code that exists somewhere in the binary, but it is not literally <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA</code>'s own machine code — a function taking eight stack arguments necessarily has a prologue that reads those arguments before doing any copying, which that sequence does not have. The more likely reconciliation is that the sequence disassembled previously is an inlined or lower-level primitive reached only for the full-screen special case, while <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA</code> itself is the general parametrized entry point documented here. The exact internal implementation (how it turns eight parameters into the appropriate <code>REP MOVSW</code>/<code>REP MOVSB</code> sequence for an arbitrary rectangle) has not been traced instruction-by-instruction and is noted as an open item rather than guessed at further.

'''ScummVM implication:''' a straightforward port should implement <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA</code> as a general <code>copyRectToScreen(buffer, pitch, dest_x, dest_y, width, height)</code> call parametrized by all eight arguments — not hardcoded to always transfer the full 320×200 frame. Since <code>dest</code> and <code>src</code> coordinates are identical in every observed call, no coordinate-translation logic is needed; the width/height/segment/offset arguments alone fully determine the operation.

=== Game loop and timing ===

No PIT (8253/8254) reprogramming was found in the binary (no <code>OUT 43h</code>/<code>OUT 40h</code> sequences), and no dedicated V-Sync polling symbol (port 0x3DA) is present. The frame rate is therefore uncapped and directly CPU-speed-dependent, in line with a great many small 1994-era DOS titles: on original period hardware this would run at roughly 10–30 fps depending on CPU class, and correspondingly faster on emulated or modern-speed hardware unless deliberately throttled. For DOSBox-based testing, a fixed low cycle count (e.g. <code>cycles=fixed 4000</code>) approximates original 8086/8088-class speed.

{{Note|'''On <code>__Int0Vector</code>/<code>__Int4Vector</code>:''' a secondary analysis source raised these two symbols (plus <code>__Int5Vector</code>, <code>__Int6Vector</code>) as evidence of an INT 08h (hardware timer) / INT 1Ch (user timer tick) hook, which would contradict the "uncapped" conclusion above. All four symbols are genuinely present in the TDS table — '''but they are not what that claim describes'''. In Borland Turbo C 2.0's runtime, <code>__IntNVector</code> names its internal table of '''CPU exception''' vectors, numbered by raw interrupt number in decimal: INT 0 (divide error), INT 4 (overflow), INT 5 (bound range exceeded), INT 6 (invalid opcode). This is the same standard CRT exception-handling scaffolding responsible for the <code>"Divide error"</code> / <code>"Abnormal program termination"</code> strings already documented elsewhere in this article — every Borland Turbo C program of this era carries it. It has no connection to the BIOS timer interrupt (INT 08h/decimal 8) or the DOS user timer tick (INT 1Ch/decimal 28); the apparent match is a numbering-base coincidence (decimal "0"/"4" read as if they were the low nibble of hex "08h"/"1Ch"). No hardware- or DOS-timer hook symbol of any kind was found, and the "uncapped, CPU-speed-dependent" conclusion above stands.}}

Input is polled, not interrupt-driven: mouse state via <code>INT 33h, AX=0003h</code> (returns button state in BX, position in CX/DX — note Mode 13h reports CX as double the pixel X coordinate, requiring a divide-by-2), keyboard via <code>_bioskey</code> (an <code>INT 16h</code> wrapper). Dialogue display (<code>_hablar</code>) busy-waits on <code>_espera_pulsar</code>/<code>_espera_soltar</code> for a mouse click, which blocks all other game-loop processing (animation, further input) for the duration — but does '''not''' block Sound Blaster DMA audio playback, which runs asynchronously on the card's own DMA channel independent of CPU activity.

=== Reconstructed control flow (pseudocode) ===

The following pseudocode reconstructs the engine's control flow from the verified symbol table and the observed call/data relationships. It is a '''behavioral reconstruction for readability, not a disassembly transcript''' — variable and function names are the real TDS symbol names, but control structure (loop shape, conditionals) is inferred, not lifted instruction-by-instruction. Where a specific step could not be confirmed, it is marked as such rather than presented as settled.

<syntaxhighlight lang="c">
// --- One-shot initialization ---
main() {
    if (!_inicializa_raton_grafico())      // INT 33h AX=0000h
        { print("No hay RATON instalado"); exit(); }

    _asigna_modo_video(0x13);              // INT 10h AH=00h AL=13h
    _asigna_memoria(...);                  // farmalloc: back-buffer, ALG buffer, VOC slots
    _INICIALIZADRV();                      // load ct-voice.drv into far heap
    _INICIALIZACMF();                      // connect to SBFMDRV.COM TSR
    _asigna_rgb(...);                      // program initial 256-color palette
    _lee_dibujos(...);                     // preload current scene's .ALG background
    _lee_ficheros_voc(...);                // preload .ALS files to _dir_voc_s1/s2/s3
    _carga_partida();                      // attempt to load an existing save, if present
    _num_room = 1;                         // start at scene 1
}

// --- Per-frame loop ---
while (!quit) {
    if (_bioskey(1))                       // INT 16h peek
        handle_key(_bioskey(0));

    if (_hare_se_mueve)
        _aumenta_num_frame();              // advance walk-cycle animation

    if (mouse_left_button_down)
        _comprueba();                      // hotspot hit-test + dispatch

    _pon_dibujos();                        // L1: background blit
    _pon_dibujos_colocao();                // L2: disc-object sprites
    _pon_hare();                           // L3: player-character sprite
    _menu_sin_volcar();                    // L4: HUD, no flip yet
    _VUELCA_PANTALLA();                    // FLIP: back-buffer -> A000:0000
}

// --- Hotspot dispatch (_comprueba), reconstructed ---
if (mouse_left_click) {
    for (each hotspot in current scene's parsed .ALD) {
        if (mouse_in_rect(hotspot.bbox)) {
            if (hotspot.is_door)
                _al_a_pantalla_k_eva(hotspot.dest_scene, hotspot.dest_door, hotspot.dest_pos);
            else {
                _coge_objeto(hotspot.object_id);
                _hablar(hotspot.dialogue_text, hotspot.als_file);
            }
            break;
        }
    }
}
</syntaxhighlight>

{{Note|'''Save/load I/O sequence — now fully confirmed by direct disassembly, resolving the earlier open question.''' <code>_graba_partida</code> (reko-decomp.txt:3936–3995) opens its target file in mode <code>"wt"</code> (text write) and writes, in order: 4 fixed <code>_fprintf</code> fields (format strings at data offsets 0x06F6, 0x06FA, 0x06FE, 0x0702) &rarr; a 16-iteration loop (<code>while(si &lt; 0x10)</code>) writing the inventory array via the format at 0x0706 &rarr; a 10-iteration loop (<code>while(si &lt; 0x0A)</code>) writing the flags array via the format at 0x070A &rarr; 2 more fixed fields (0x070E, then offset 1810) &rarr; <code>_fclose</code>. <code>_carga_partida</code> performs the exact inverse with <code>_fscanf</code> in mode <code>"rt"</code>. This directly confirms, at the code level rather than only from inspecting output files, that the earlier-debunked <code>_codifica</code>/XOR-0xFF claim for this routine is wrong — the routine is plain-text <code>fprintf</code>/<code>fscanf</code> throughout, exactly matching the plain-text structure already confirmed in the real <code>GAMESAVE</code>/<code>AUXILIO</code>/<code>AUXILIAR</code> files. It also gives the inventory and flag arrays their real, confirmed sizes: '''16 inventory slots, 10 flag slots''' — more precise than this article's earlier "variable length" description. The filename itself is passed in by the caller (<code>_para_grabar</code>, bound to the F1 key per the confirmed main-loop description above) as a pointer to a data-segment string; resolving that exact segment-relative offset to a specific one of <code>"gamesave"</code>/<code>"auxilio"</code> was not completed here and is left as the one remaining open item on this question, rather than guessed at.}}

{{Note|'''Correction — the main-loop CALL/JMP addresses are confirmed.''' A previous revision of this article attempted to verify these addresses by adding the 512-byte header size to each logical address before locating it in the file, found no <code>CALL</code> opcode at any of them, and concluded they could not be confirmed. '''That offset convention was itself wrong.''' Using the correct convention — file offset equals the logical address directly, with no header addition — all seventeen claimed addresses (the eight originally listed, later extended to seventeen by a follow-up source) resolve exactly to the claimed opcode (<code>0x9A</code> far call or <code>0xE8</code> near call), and every near-call's relative displacement independently computes to the exact claimed target address. This is one of the more useful corrections in this article's own history: a secondary source's specific, checkable claim turned out to be right, and this article's initial skepticism was the error. The confirmed jump-table/dispatcher mechanism these calls form is described in detail under [[#Cross-verification log|Cross-verification log]], along with why it does not constitute a general bytecode interpreter despite one source's framing of it that way.}}

=== Character and animation subsystem ===

Consolidating every confirmed symbol touching Paco's on-screen representation into one coherent specification (individual symbols are cross-referenced to their fuller descriptions under [[#HARE.EXE|HARE.EXE]]):

{| class="wikitable"
! State variable !! Role
|-
| <code>_hare_x</code>, <code>_hare_y</code> || Current pixel position, 0–319 / 0–199
|-
| <code>_hare_se_mueve</code> || Boolean: currently walking vs. idle. Gates whether <code>_aumenta_num_frame</code> advances the walk cycle at all
|-
| <code>_sentido_hare</code> || Facing direction: 0 = left (selects <code>_dir_hare_izq</code> sprite data), 1 = right (selects <code>_dir_hare_dch</code>)
|-
| <code>_num_frame</code> || Current walk-cycle frame index
|-
| <code>_frame_x</code>, <code>_frame_y</code> || Sprite-sheet pixel offset corresponding to the current <code>_num_frame</code> value — i.e. the lookup from frame index to sheet coordinates is precomputed into these two variables rather than recomputed from a formula each frame
|-
| <code>_dir_hare_dch</code>, <code>_dir_hare_izq</code> || Far pointers to the player-character sprite-sheet data, one per facing direction. '''Neither sprite sheet has been located in any known copy of the distribution''' — this is the single largest visual gap for a faithful reimplementation, larger in practical impact than the missing <code>99.ALG</code>, since Paco is on-screen in every scene
|}

Non-player figures use a parallel, simpler position-only state (no separate walk-cycle machinery was found for them, consistent with NPCs in this engine being static art rather than animated characters):

{| class="wikitable"
! Variable !! Role
|-
| <code>_x_figura1</code>, <code>_y_figura1</code> || Position of the first non-Paco figure — most plausibly Mariano, given Scene 11's single large object hotspot (34,35)–(140,109)
|-
| <code>_x_figura2</code>, <code>_y_figura2</code> || Position of a second figure slot
|-
| <code>_x_figura3</code> || Position (X only confirmed present) of a third figure slot
|}

'''Movement model:''' no pathfinding of any kind is implemented — <code>_lleva_al_hare(tx, ty)</code> (see the pseudocode under [[#Reconstructed control flow (pseudocode)|Reconstructed control flow]]) is a direct linear interpolation from the current position toward the click target, unconditionally, with no obstacle avoidance and no concept of a walkable-area mask distinct from the simple "below y≈148 is HUD/dialogue territory" rule already noted under [[#Rendering pipeline|Rendering pipeline]]. A reimplementation that matches the original's feel should '''not''' add pathfinding around obstacles — doing so would be a deviation from, not an improvement matching, the source material's actual behavior. Where a reimplementation legitimately can exceed the original without changing observable behavior: sub-pixel movement interpolation for smoother animation at high frame rates, since the original's per-frame integer stepping was itself a product of the uncapped, CPU-speed-dependent timing already documented, not a deliberate aesthetic choice.

== File formats ==

All formats below were decoded and independently verified — either by successfully rendering/parsing every available sample file, or, where noted, cross-checked directly against the original QuickBASIC editor source that generates them.

=== .ALG — scene backgrounds ===

Standard '''PCX (ZSoft) version 3.0''', 320×200, 8 bits per pixel (256-color, single plane), RLE-compressed, with a trailing VGA palette. No deviation from the public PCX v3.0 specification was found; any existing PCX decoder handles these files without modification.

{| class="wikitable"
! Field !! Value
|-
| Header || 128 bytes, fixed
|-
| Manufacturer / version / encoding bytes || 0x0A / 0x05 / 0x01
|-
| Bounding box || (0,0)–(319,199) in every sample
|-
| Planes || 1 (8-bit paletted, not 4-plane EGA)
|-
| RLE rule || byte ≥ 0xC0 → run of (byte AND 0x3F) copies of the next byte; else literal byte
|-
| Palette || 768 bytes (256 × RGB, 0–255 range) preceded by marker byte 0x0C, located at (file size − 769)
|-
| Decompressed size || exactly 64,000 bytes (320 × 200 × 1)
|}

==== Reference decoder (complete) ====

The following is sufficient, on its own, to decode every <code>.ALG</code> file in the corpus with zero modification. It has been run end-to-end against all five available background files with byte-exact results (see the compression-ratio table below).

<syntaxhighlight lang="c">
#define ALG_WIDTH  320
#define ALG_HEIGHT 200
#define ALG_HEADER_SIZE 128
#define ALG_PALETTE_SIZE 768

// buf: full raw file contents. out_pixels: caller-allocated 64000-byte buffer.
// out_palette: caller-allocated 768-byte buffer.
void decode_alg(const uint8_t *buf, size_t file_size,
                 uint8_t *out_pixels, uint8_t *out_palette) {

    // --- Header fields actually needed (all others are fixed/ignored) ---
    uint16_t xmin = read_le16(buf + 4),  ymin = read_le16(buf + 6);
    uint16_t xmax = read_le16(buf + 8),  ymax = read_le16(buf + 10);
    uint16_t bytes_per_line = read_le16(buf + 66);   // may exceed ALG_WIDTH (row padding)
    int width  = xmax - xmin + 1;                     // == 320 for every known .ALG
    int height = ymax - ymin + 1;                      // == 200 for every known .ALG

    // --- Palette: last 769 bytes of the file: [0x0C marker][256 x RGB] ---
    assert(buf[file_size - 769] == 0x0C);
    memcpy(out_palette, buf + file_size - 768, ALG_PALETTE_SIZE);

    // --- RLE decompress into a scratch buffer sized height*bytes_per_line ---
    size_t needed = (size_t)height * bytes_per_line;
    uint8_t *scratch = malloc(needed);
    size_t src = ALG_HEADER_SIZE, dst = 0;
    while (dst < needed) {
        uint8_t b = buf[src++];
        if ((b & 0xC0) == 0xC0) {              // run-length byte
            int count = b & 0x3F;              // 1..63 repeats
            uint8_t value = buf[src++];
            while (count-- > 0) scratch[dst++] = value;
        } else {                                // literal byte
            scratch[dst++] = b;
        }
    }

    // --- Strip row padding: keep only the first ALG_WIDTH bytes of each row ---
    for (int y = 0; y < height; y++)
        memcpy(out_pixels + y * ALG_WIDTH,
               scratch + y * bytes_per_line,
               ALG_WIDTH);

    free(scratch);
}
</syntaxhighlight>

The one-line VGA-DAC caveat this decoder deliberately does '''not''' apply: <code>out_palette</code> values are 0–255, suitable for direct use with a modern 8-bit-per-channel <code>Graphics::Surface</code> or SDL palette. Only if driving real (or precisely emulated) VGA hardware through ports 0x3C8/0x3C9 does each channel need an additional <code>>> 2</code> shift to fit the DAC's 6-bit range — see [[#Rendering pipeline|Rendering pipeline]].

|-
| <code>1.ALG</code> || 20,466 || 68.02% || Scene 1 background
|-

=== .ALS — dialogue audio ===

'''Creative Labs Voice File format, version 1.10''' (the classic "VOC" format). PCM 8-bit unsigned, mono. Two sample rates are used across the corpus: '''21,739 Hz''' (divisor byte 0xD2 = 210; used by every numbered <code>N.ALS</code> file) and '''10,989 Hz''' (divisor byte 0xA5 = 165; used only by the unnumbered file <code>07</code>, a 16.7-second narration, likely intro/outro material).

{| class="wikitable"
! Offset !! Size !! Content
|-
| 0 || 19 B || <code>"Creative Voice File"</code> (no null terminator)
|-
| 19 || 1 B || <code>0x1A</code> (EOF marker)
|-
| 20 || 2 B LE || Header size (always 0x001A = 26)
|-
| 22 || 2 B LE || Version (<code>0x010A</code> = 1.10)
|-
| 24 || 2 B LE || Version checksum (<code>~version + 0x1234</code>)
|-
| 26+ || varies || Data blocks: 1-byte type, 3-byte LE length, then payload. Type <code>0x01</code> = PCM audio (payload begins with 1-byte rate divisor + 1-byte codec, then raw samples); type <code>0x00</code> = terminator (no length field)
|}

Any existing VOC decoder (ScummVM's <code>Audio::makeVOCStream</code> included) handles this format without modification.

==== Reference decoder (complete) ====

<syntaxhighlight lang="c">
// Returns malloc'd PCM buffer via *out_pcm (caller frees); returns sample count.
// *out_rate receives the sample rate for this file.
size_t decode_als(const uint8_t *buf, size_t file_size,
                   uint8_t **out_pcm, uint32_t *out_rate) {

    assert(memcmp(buf, "Creative Voice File", 19) == 0);
    uint16_t header_size = read_le16(buf + 20);   // always 26 (0x001A) in this corpus

    size_t pos = header_size;
    uint8_t *pcm = NULL;
    size_t pcm_len = 0;
    uint32_t rate = 0;

    while (pos < file_size) {
        uint8_t block_type = buf[pos++];
        if (block_type == 0x00) break;             // terminator, no length field

        uint32_t block_len = buf[pos] | (buf[pos+1] << 8) | (buf[pos+2] << 16);
        pos += 3;

        if (block_type == 0x01) {                  // PCM sound data
            uint8_t divisor = buf[pos];
            uint8_t codec   = buf[pos + 1];         // 0x00 = unsigned 8-bit PCM (only value seen)
            rate = 1000000UL / (256 - divisor);     // 210 -> 21739 Hz; 165 -> 10989 Hz

            uint32_t sample_count = block_len - 2;
            pcm = realloc(pcm, pcm_len + sample_count);
            memcpy(pcm + pcm_len, buf + pos + 2, sample_count);
            pcm_len += sample_count;
        }
        // block types 0x02 (silence), 0x03 (marker), 0x06/0x07 (repeat begin/end),
        // 0x08 (extended, stereo/higher-rate) are part of the VOC 1.10 spec but were
        // not observed in any .ALS file in this corpus — type 0x01 is the only
        // block type actually encountered.

        pos += block_len;
    }

    *out_pcm = pcm;
    *out_rate = rate;
    return pcm_len;
}

// Unsigned 8-bit -> signed 16-bit, for audio APIs (e.g. ScummVM's mixer,
// SDL_AudioSpec) that expect signed samples:
//   s16 = (u8 - 128) << 8
</syntaxhighlight>

=== .CMF — background music (now fully verified against all five real files) ===

{{Note|'''This section supersedes an earlier draft''' that could only describe the public Creative Music Format specification in the abstract, with an explicit caveat that no <code>.CMF</code> sample from this game had been available for inspection. All five referenced/used CMF files — <code>AULD.CMF</code>, <code>STARFM.CMF</code>, <code>JUEGO.CMF</code>, <code>RANGE.CMF</code>, and <code>ALLE.CMF</code> — have since been obtained and are verified below byte-for-byte, from the complete original DOSBox distribution package. The evidentiary caveat is retired; the header specification below is confirmed exact.}}

CMF (Creative Music Format) is a MIDI-like sequence format for driving the OPL2 FM synthesis chip. Every field in the specification table below is confirmed present at the stated offset in all five real files:

{| class="wikitable"
! Offset !! Size !! Field !! Confirmed value (all 5 files)
|-
| 0x00 || 4 B || Magic || <code>"CTMF"</code>, exact, all five files
|-
| 0x04 || 2 B LE || Format version || <code>0x0101</code> (v1.1) in all five files
|-
| 0x06 || 2 B LE || Instrument-patch block offset || present and internally consistent (block begins immediately after the header)
|-
| 0x08 || 2 B LE || Music-sequence (event) block offset || confirmed; sequence data begins cleanly at this offset in all five files
|-
| 0x0A || 2 B LE || Ticks per quarter note || present, non-zero, plausible tempo-grid values in all five files
|-
| 0x0C || 2 B LE || Ticks per second (playback timebase) || present; used directly below for duration estimates
|-
| 0x0E || 2 B LE || Title/composer/remarks tag block offset || non-zero in 4 of 5 files (only <code>AULD.CMF</code> has no tag block); see the tag-content finding below
|}

==== Per-file measurements ====

{| class="wikitable"
! File !! Size (bytes) !! Tag block !! Estimated duration !! Channels used !! Scene(s) it plays in
|-
| <code>AULD.CMF</code> || (confirmed CTMF v1.1) || none (offset 0) || '''unreliable — see note''' || 0,1,2,3,4,5,11,12,15 || Scenes 1–4 (per <code>.ALD</code> line 2)
|-
| <code>STARFM.CMF</code> || (confirmed CTMF v1.1) || present, content inconclusive || ≈1m 26.6s || 0,1,2,3,4,5,11,12,15 || Scenes 8–9 (per <code>.ALD</code> line 2)
|-
| <code>JUEGO.CMF</code> || (confirmed CTMF v1.1) || present, content inconclusive || ≈2m 31.5s || 0 only (single-channel) || Slot-machine mini-game (per embedded filename string, see [[#Embedded strings and file references|Embedded strings and file references]])
|-
| <code>RANGE.CMF</code> || (confirmed CTMF v1.1) || '''present, decodes cleanly: "LITTLE BROWN JUG"''' || '''unreliable — see note''' || 0–15 (all 16 channels) || Scene 7 (per <code>.ALD</code> line 2)
|-
| <code>ALLE.CMF</code> || (confirmed CTMF v1.1) || present, content inconclusive || ≈2m 58.2s || 0–8,11,12,14,15 || Scenes 5–6 (per <code>.ALD</code> line 2)
|}

{{Note|'''Duration estimates are heuristic, not a full sequencer.''' Duration was estimated by summing all delta-times in the sequence block (standard MIDI-style variable-length quantities) and dividing by the ticks-per-second header field. This produced plausible results (1–3 minutes, appropriate for a looping background track) for <code>STARFM.CMF</code>, <code>JUEGO.CMF</code>, and <code>ALLE.CMF</code>, but produced implausible multi-hour figures for <code>AULD.CMF</code> and <code>RANGE.CMF</code> — including after adding MIDI running-status handling to the walker. This means the simplified event-walker desynchronizes somewhere in those two files' event streams (most likely on an event type it doesn't correctly skip past), not that those two tracks are actually hours long. A correct duration for these two requires a proper stateful CMF/MIDI sequencer, not a further round of heuristic patching — this is noted as an open item rather than papered over with a wrong number.}}

==== Major correction: RANGE.CMF and ALLE.CMF are real, actively-used game music ====

{{Note|'''This retracts a specific conclusion from the previous revision of this article.''' Because <code>RANGE.CMF</code> and <code>ALLE.CMF</code> do not appear as hardcoded filename strings anywhere in <code>HARE.EXE</code> (only <code>"AULD.CMF"</code> and <code>"STARFM.CMF"</code> are hardcoded there), the previous revision concluded they were "unreferenced, orphaned development/test assets — plausibly stock library files." '''This was incorrect.''' Now that the complete scene set (all eleven scenes) has been obtained and every <code>.ALD</code> file's line 2 (music filename) has been read directly, both files are confirmed as the real, actively-loaded background music for specific scenes: Scenes 5 and 6 load <code>ALLE.CMF</code>; Scene 7 loads <code>RANGE.CMF</code>. The error in the earlier analysis was searching only the executable's own hardcoded string table and failing to account for the fact that '''most''' scene music filenames are supplied dynamically, per-scene, from <code>.ALD</code> data rather than being hardcoded in the binary at all — only the two most common tracks (<code>AULD.CMF</code>, used by the four-scene 1–4 cluster, and <code>STARFM.CMF</code>, used by the 8–9 cluster) happened to also appear as literal strings elsewhere in the binary, which is what created the false impression that the other two were unused.}}

Separately and remarkably: <code>RANGE.CMF</code>'s tag block decodes cleanly (unlike the other three tagged files, whose tag regions do not decode as clean text under either a null-terminated or length-prefixed reading — left as an open discrepancy rather than forced) to the literal title '''"LITTLE BROWN JUG"''' — the name of a well-known 19th-century American folk tune. Given the track is confirmed as genuine, actively-loaded Scene 7 music rather than a discarded test file, the most likely explanation is that the composer built (or adapted) Scene 7's chiptune arrangement starting from a stock/library MIDI or CMF arrangement of that public-domain tune and never updated the embedded tag — a common, mundane practice, not evidence of anything unusual about the scene itself.

==== ScummVM path ====

No CMF-specific parser needs to be written from scratch — ScummVM already ships OPL2 emulation (<code>audio/fmopl.h</code>) suitable for consuming the register-level data this format encodes; only a thin CMF sequence-to-register-write translator is needed on top of it (see [[#Reusable ScummVM subsystems|Reusable ScummVM subsystems]]).

=== .ALD — scene layout data ===

The central data-driven format of the engine, and the one requiring the most care to reproduce exactly. Plain ASCII text, CRLF-line-delimited, encrypted at rest with a trivial whole-byte XOR against <code>0xFF</code> (equivalent to a bitwise NOT — the same operation reverses it). The in-game routine responsible, named <code>_codifica</code> in the TDS symbol table, is a two-line loop with no keying material; this is obfuscation against casual hex-editor viewing, not security.

The format was cross-verified against the actual level-editor source (<code>SCOVA.ALC</code>, a QuickBASIC 4.5 program — see [[#Development tools|below]]), specifically its <code>FUNCTION GRABAR</code>, which writes exactly this layout:

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
Line 1:  scene ID string                    (e.g. "1", "10", "11")
Line 2:  music filename                     (e.g. "AULD.CMF", "STARFM.CMF")
Line 3:  NOP  — count of on-screen objects (hotspots and doors)
Line 4:  NOD  — count of disc-object sprites (from the 99.ALG sheet)

[Repeat NOP times:]
  object ID (integer, globally unique)
  X1, Y1                                    (hotspot top-left, 0–319 / 0–199)
  X2, Y2                                    (hotspot bottom-right)
  PUER                                      (0 = interactive object, 1 = door/exit)
  [only if PUER = 1:]
    destination scene filename              (e.g. "5.ALD")
    destination door ID
    destination entry position              (0 = left, 1 = right, 2 = center)

"99"                                        (literal terminator string)

[Repeat NOD times:]
  sprite index in 99.ALG (0-based column)
  sheet X1, Y1
  sheet X2  (= X1 + 39)
  sheet Y2  (= Y1 + 39 — SEE BUG NOTE BELOW)
  scene placement X, Y
</syntaxhighlight>

{{Note|'''Known source bug, verified against SCOVA.ALC:''' <code>FUNCTION GRABAR</code> computes the disc-object sheet's bottom edge as <code>POY(I) + TAMANIOX(0)</code> — it reuses the '''width''' constant (<code>TAMANIOX = 39</code>) for the '''height''' field instead of the correct height constant (<code>TAMANIOY = 24</code>), which is confirmed elsewhere in the same source via its <code>GET</code> statement bounds. Every disc-object sheet rectangle in every <code>.ALD</code> file therefore encodes a bottom edge 15 pixels too far down. A conforming decoder must ignore the stored Y2 for height purposes and use a fixed sprite height of 24 pixels.}}

Line-ending detail for implementers: QuickBASIC's <code>PRINT #1</code> writes CRLF (<code>0x0D 0x0A</code>); after XOR-0xFF these become <code>0xF2 0xF5</code> on disk. Integer fields are written with a leading and trailing space (e.g. <code>" 42 "</code>) — strip whitespace before parsing.

The five scenes available in early analysis passes (1, 2, 3, 10, 11) originally parsed into an apparently linear chain with two unexplained loose ends: Scene 1's door to an unreachable "Scene 5," and Scene 10's puzzle-blocked door to an unreachable "Scene 9." Both are now explained. The complete original distribution (all eleven scenes) has since been obtained, and every <code>.ALD</code> file has been parsed directly:

{| class="wikitable"
! Scene !! Music !! Objects !! Notable connectivity
|-
| 1 || AULD.CMF || 2 doors || → scene 2 (left entry); → scene 5 (center entry) — '''resolved''': scene 5 is a real, reachable hub room
|-
| 2 || AULD.CMF || 2 doors, 1 disc-object || ↔ scenes 1, 3; disc-object sprite #4
|-
| 3 || AULD.CMF || 2 doors, 1 disc-object || ↔ scenes 2, 4; disc-object sprite #3
|-
| 4 || AULD.CMF || 1 door, 1 disc-object || '''dead-end''' off scene 3 only; disc-object sprite #14
|-
| 5 || AULD.CMF (entry) / ALLE.CMF || 2 doors, 1 object || '''junction room''': ↔ scene 1 (right) '''and''' ↔ scene 6 (left) — the two clusters of the game connect here
|-

|-
| 7 || RANGE.CMF || 3 doors, 5 disc-objects || '''junction room''': ↔ scene 6, '''and''' branches to both scene 8 '''and''' scene 9; disc-object sprites #2, #6, #9, #11, #15 (the richest single scene for disc-objects in the game)

{{Note|'''This corrects the previous, partial-data conclusion in this article''' that the game's scenes formed "an entirely linear and single-branch" sequence. That conclusion was reached honestly from the five scenes available at the time, but the complete eleven-scene picture shows two genuine junction rooms (5 and 7), each connecting three neighbors rather than two. See also the correction to the Puzzle flag state machine section below, and the major <code>RANGE.CMF</code>/<code>ALLE.CMF</code> correction under [[#.CMF — background music (now fully verified against all five real files)|.CMF]] — both scene 5's and scene 7's music assignments were the missing piece that made this topology fully legible.}}

=== Save format — GAMESAVE, AUXILIO, AUXILIAR ===

{{Note|This section documents a save-format investigation still in progress. Everything stated as fact below was checked directly against three sample files; two open questions are flagged explicitly as open rather than resolved. A prior draft of this analysis asserted more than the evidence supported and has been corrected — see the note at the end of this subsection.}}

Three save-format files are known: <code>GAMESAVE</code> (104 bytes), <code>AUXILIO</code> (104 bytes), and <code>AUXILIAR</code> (164 bytes). All three are '''plain ASCII text, CRLF-delimited — not XOR-0xFF encrypted''' (every byte is printable or a CRLF pair; attempting the <code>.ALD</code>-style XOR decode produces high-bit garbage, not text). This is a materially different on-disk convention from <code>.ALD</code> and should not be assumed to share the same encoding.

All three share an identical header shape:

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
Line 0:  scene reference filename        (all three samples: "6.ALD")
Line 1:  integer, diverges per file      (124 / 148 / 214 across the three samples)
Line 2:  integer, constant = 64 in all three samples
Line 3+: integer array (flag/inventory-like state), variable length
</syntaxhighlight>

No terminator sentinel exists in any of the three files — the array simply ends at EOF.

'''Open question 1 — the meaning of the divergent header integer (Line 1) and the constant 64 (Line 2):''' plausible but unconfirmed without disassembly of the actual save routine. A monotonic counter (elapsed ticks or moves) is the most consistent reading of Line 1, given three distinct, non-repeating values across three saves at the same scene; 64 is consistent with a fixed array-size constant.

'''Open question 2 — what "auxilio" means inside HARE.EXE:''' the literal strings <code>auxilio\0 98.alg\0 auxilio\0</code> appear together in the game's data segment, adjacent to the dialogue-string table. Two explanations are equally consistent with the evidence and neither is confirmed:
# It is spoken/displayed text ("Help!") tied to a distinct <code>98.alg</code> screen, unconnected to the save files of the same name.
# It is literally the base filename <code>HARE.EXE</code>'s own save routine writes to for a secondary slot.

Grep of both known level-editor sources (<code>CACA.ALC</code> and <code>SCOVA2.ALC</code>) turns up '''zero''' references to the strings <code>"auxilio"</code>, <code>"AUXILIAR"</code>, or <code>"gamesave"</code> anywhere in either tool — so neither editor is the program writing these files under those names; whatever writes them is <code>HARE.EXE</code> itself or an unexamined third tool. This document does not assert a winner between the two hypotheses above; resolving it needs disassembly of the code path around the save routine, which is out of scope for a strings-and-structure pass.

{{Note|Correction: an earlier pass at this analysis, made before the three save files above were available for direct inspection, incorrectly asserted (a) that a specific 104-byte range inside <code>HARE.EXE</code>'s data segment ''was'' an embedded savegame buffer, and (b) that the save format used a distinctive terminator value. Neither survives inspection of the real files: the cited byte range sits arbitrarily inside a run of null padding with no structural marker, and no such terminator appears in any real save file. Both claims are retracted here for the record.}}

{{Note|'''Second re-verification, against a later secondary source repeating the same claim:''' a subsequent analysis document reasserted the 0xC628–0xC68F "save buffer" theory, this time with specific supporting detail — claiming byte 0x62 of that range equals <code>0x0F</code> ("a Mariano-NPC marker") and byte 0x65 equals <code>0x23</code> ("an NPC-satisfied marker"). Direct re-inspection of the real bytes at those exact offsets shows byte 0x62 = <code>0xB1</code> and byte 0x65 = <code>0x5F</code> — '''neither matches the claimed value'''. The values <code>0x0F</code> and <code>0x23</code> do appear elsewhere in that same 104-byte window, just not at the cited offsets, consistent with the claim having been constructed from real bytes in the vicinity without a precise offset-to-byte check. Combined with the structural argument above (the range starts inside null padding with no boundary marker), this claim is considered closed rather than merely open. The repeated trailing pattern <code>B1 5F</code> ×3 at the very end of the window is real and unexplained — most consistent with a fragment of an unrelated lookup/index table (see the object–action table discussion under [[#HARE.EXE|HARE.EXE]]) rather than a save-state checksum.}}

=== 99.ALG — shared sprite sheet (now obtained; geometry solved and verified against real pixels) ===

{{Note|'''This section supersedes two earlier revisions.''' The first draft guessed "2 rows × 8 columns"; a later revision corrected this to a source-cited "7 columns, 2 rows" reconstruction derived purely from reading <code>SCOVA.ALC</code>'s <code>GET</code> statements, with no access to the actual file, and spent uncertain on whether the two rows represented 14 distinct sprites or 2 visual states of the same 7 objects. The file (distributed without its <code>.ALG</code> extension, as bare filename <code>99</code>) has since been obtained from the complete original distribution. Every prediction from the source-code-only reconstruction is now confirmed exactly against the real pixel data, '''and''' the two-states speculation is resolved: it is 14 distinct sprites, not 7 objects × 2 states.}}

'''Column geometry — confirmed exactly against real pixels.''' Sampling the center pixel of all 28 predicted cells (7 columns × 4 rows: 2 sprite rows + 2 mask rows) against a background reference found genuine, distinct artwork in '''100% of cells''' (28/28), with no empty cells and no repeating/desynchronized content:

{| class="wikitable"
! ELEC (column) !! X1 !! X2 !! Width
|-
| 1 || 2 || 41 || 39
|-
| 2 || 43 || 82 || 39
|-
| 3 || 84 || 123 || 39
|-
| 4 || 125 || 164 || 39
|-
| 5 || 166 || 205 || 39
|-
| 6 || 207 || 246 || 39
|-
| 7 || 248 || 287 || 39
|}
Confirmed: exactly 7 columns (a hypothetical 8th would run to X=328, past the 320px canvas edge — this was correctly predicted before the file was available and now stands confirmed).

'''Row geometry — confirmed exactly:'''

{| class="wikitable"
! Row !! Y1 !! Y2 !! Height !! Role
|-
| Sprite row 1 || 17 || 41 || 24 || Sprite indices 2–8
|-
| Sprite row 2 || 43 || 67 || 24 || Sprite indices 9–15
|-
| Mask row 1 || 73 || 97 || 24 || Mask for sprite row 1 (Y offset +56 from 17)
|-
| Mask row 2 || 99 || 123 || 24 || Mask for sprite row 2 (Y offset +56 from 43)
|}

'''The complete sprite-index formula — solved empirically''' by tabulating every <code>(sprite_index, sheet_x1, sheet_y1)</code> triple recorded across all eleven scenes' <code>.ALD</code> disc-object records (11 confirmed data points, once the complete scene set was available) and solving for the column/row/index relationship directly, rather than continuing to guess:

{| class="wikitable"
! Sprite index !! Row !! Column (ELEC) !! Confirmed from scene
|-
| 2 || row 1 || 1 || Scene 7
|-
| 3 || row 1 || 2 || Scene 3
|-
| 4 || row 1 || 3 || Scene 2
|-
| 5 || row 1 || 4 || Scene 8
|-
| 6 || row 1 || 5 || Scene 7
|-
| 7 || row 1 || 6 || Scene 5
|-
| 9 || row 2 || 1 || Scene 7
|-
| 11 || row 2 || 2 || Scene 7
|-
| 13 || row 2 || 4 || Scene 9
|-
| 14 || row 2 || 5 || Scene 4
|-
| 15 || row 2 || 6 || Scene 7
|}

The clean, complete formula: '''row 1 index = column + 1''' (columns 1–7 → indices 2–8); '''row 2 index = column + 8''' (columns 1–7 → indices 9–15). '''Sprite index 1 is never used''' by any disc-object in any of the eleven scenes — plausibly reserved, or corresponding to a sheet position not used as a placeable disc-object (e.g. Paco's own sprite data, stored on the same sheet but referenced by the separate <code>_dir_hare_dch</code>/<code>_dir_hare_izq</code> pointers rather than by <code>NUOD</code> index).

'''Retraction: the "two visual states of 7 objects" hypothesis is wrong.''' The earlier draft speculated that the two rows might represent two states (on/off, open/closed) of the same 7 puzzle objects, since only 2 real sheet coordinates were available to check at the time. With 11 real data points now in hand, rows 1 and 2 are confirmed to encode '''14 independently-addressable sprites''' (indices 2–15, contiguous), used across different scenes for different purposes (food items, a key, a book, tools, a lever/wrench, a basket — see the visual description below) — not two states of a smaller set of 7. The mask-row content also does not show the uniform black/white transparency-key pattern a simple 1-bit mask would produce, which is noted as an open detail rather than forced into the original "transparency mask" framing; treat the mask rows as "a second full-color image per sprite, whose exact compositing role is not yet re-derived from the real pixels," pending closer study.

'''Visual content, now directly observable:''' the fourteen sprites are recognizable everyday objects consistent with the game's inventory-driven puzzles — among them a red book, a bottle with a green-and-red label, a wrapped/strawy bundle, a plank of wood, a gold key, a loaf of bread, a piece of cured meat, a wire/mesh grate, a red glove or mitt, a wrench or pipe fitting, and a woven basket. This is a plain-language description of what is visible in the decoded sheet, not a claim about which specific dialogue line or puzzle step each one corresponds to — that mapping is a natural next step now that the asset exists, but is not asserted here without tracing each sprite index back to its specific disc-object placement and any dialogue triggered on pickup.

[[File:Paco1994_SpriteSheet99_Annotated.svg|thumb|center|700px|The complete <code>99.ALG</code> sprite sheet with the solved column/row/index formula overlaid on the real decoded pixel data. Green boxes: row 1 (indices 2–8). Orange boxes: row 2 (indices 9–15). Blue boxes: the two corresponding mask rows.]]

=== SALCHI1–4.LBM — IFF ILBM background art ===

Standard '''IFF ILBM''' (InterLeaved BitMap), 320×200, 8 bitplanes (256 colors), <code>ByteRun1</code> (PackBits-style) RLE compression, standard row-interleaved-by-plane layout with plane 0 as the least-significant bit. Also present: <code>DPPV</code> and four <code>CRNG</code> (color-cycle range) auxiliary chunks from Deluxe Paint; the <code>CRNG</code> ranges are flagged inactive in every sample and do not affect single-frame decoding. RLE decompression was verified byte-exact against all four files (compressed input fully consumed, exactly 64,000 decompressed bytes produced, zero leftover). The decoded artwork is dense, heavily dithered 1994-era VGA background material — an initial visual impression of "noise" during decoding turned out to be a subjective misreading of legitimate detailed pixel art, not a decode defect, and was corrected after closer inspection.

=== Short VOC effects: S1–S4 ===

Four additional Creative VOC v1.10 files, 0.32–2.37 seconds each — too short to be spoken dialogue lines. Consistent with UI or slot-machine sound effects; not yet matched to a specific trigger.

=== Unresolved: TITULOS2.ANM ===

Begins with the four bytes <code>LPF </code> rather than the standard IFF <code>FORM</code> magic. Not decoded; flagged for a dedicated follow-up pass rather than guessed at here.

== Executables ==

=== HARE.EXE ===

The primary game executable (81,179 bytes). Contains the complete puzzle logic, all dialogue text, and — via its appended Borland TDS debug-symbol section — 348 named public symbols (boundary-safe count; see the methodology note under [[#Toolchain identification|Toolchain identification]]), which is the single most valuable static artifact available: it effectively documents the entire engine's internal function and variable names without requiring blind disassembly. A representative selection:

{| class="wikitable"
! Symbol !! Role
|-
| <code>_setvgapalette256</code> || Writes 256 RGB triplets to the VGA DAC (ports 0x3C8/0x3C9)
|-
| <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA</code> || Page flip: back-buffer → VRAM
|-
| <code>_DIBUJA_BLOQUE_CON_MASK</code> || Masked sprite blit
|-
| <code>_lee_dibujos</code> / <code>_descomprime_dibujo</code> || PCX load + RLE decompress
|-
| <code>_codifica</code> || XOR-0xFF buffer transform (used for <code>.ALD</code> decode)
|-
| <code>_hablar</code> / <code>_habla_mariano</code> || Dialogue box display + VOC playback + click-to-continue wait
|-
| <code>_al_a_pantalla_k_eva</code> / <code>_sal_de_la_habitacion</code> || Scene transition in/out
|-
| <code>_comprueba</code> / <code>_comprueba1</code> / <code>_comprueba2</code> || Hotspot hit-test and puzzle dispatch
|-

A full 120-symbol annotated table with inferred C signatures is maintained as a companion reference (see [[#References and further material|references]]).

'''The slot-machine function itself, and a resolved question about <code>_escoba</code>/<code>_carga_escoba</code>:''' direct reading of the real <code>HARE.EXE</code> Reko decompilation locates the slot machine's own dedicated function, <code>_tragaperras(cx, dx, ds)</code>, and settles a specific disagreement that arose while cross-checking a secondary source's claims:

{| class="wikitable"
! Symbol !! Confirmed role
|-
| <code>_tragaperras</code> || The slot-machine mini-game's own function body. It calls the same general-purpose <code>_pon_dibujos</code> (background redraw) and <code>_comprueba</code> (hotspot hit-test) primitives the main game uses — this is expected, not evidence of a separate rendering system, and should not be mistaken for the main game loop merely because both call the same rendering functions.
|-
| <code>_escoba</code> || {{Note|'''Self-correction: this article's own earlier verdict here was wrong.''' An initial pass read the function's opening lines (mouse init, then a call into <code>_carga_escoba</code>) and a closing <code>do{...}while(flag != 1)</code> condition, but did not read the loop body itself, and concluded on that basis that a single call site ruled out this being the main loop — a reasoning error, since being called once and then looping internally is exactly how a main loop normally works. Reading the full loop body (reko-decomp.txt:2758–2815) settles it: '''this is the main game loop.''' Each iteration: hides the mouse cursor (<code>_desactiva_raton</code>) &rarr; calls <code>_mueve_objeto</code> (slot-machine reel animation) or <code>_refresca_pantalla</code> depending on a mode flag &rarr; builds the full-screen <code>_VUELCA_PANTALLA(0,0,0,0,320,199,seg,off)</code> call and executes it &rarr; restores the cursor (<code>_activa_raton</code>) &rarr; polls the mouse via <code>INT 33h</code> &rarr; dispatches to <code>_comprueba1</code> (normal mode) or <code>_comprueba2</code> (slot-machine mode) depending on the same flag &rarr; polls the keyboard via <code>_bioskey</code>, checking scancode <code>0x3B</code> (F1) &rarr; <code>_para_grabar</code> (save) and <code>0x3C</code> (F2) &rarr; <code>_para_cargar</code> (load) — '''newly confirmed: F1/F2 are the save/load keyboard shortcuts''', not previously documented. The loop exits when a flag is set to 1 (quit). <code>_carga_escoba</code>'s file-parsing role, called once before the loop begins, stands as previously described.}}
|-
| <code>_carga_escoba</code> || Larger and more general than its name suggests: its body uses <code>_fopen</code>/<code>_fscanf</code>/<code>_strcpy</code> against a filename passed in as an argument (a far pointer, e.g. <code>SEQ(ds, 0x04D5)</code> at its one call site inside <code>_escoba</code>), and is called from '''four''' separate locations in the code with (presumably) different filename arguments each time. This reads much more like a generic "open this text file and parse fixed fields from it via <code>fscanf</code>" utility than a function specifically about loading a broom sprite — the original "broom" interpretation (drawn from the TDS symbol table's naming alone) may describe only its '''first''', historical use, not its full role. Exactly which file(s) it is used to parse beyond the one call inside <code>_escoba</code> has not been traced further; this is flagged as an open, promising lead rather than a resolved fact.
|}

A secondary analysis source claimed, with high confidence, that <code>_escoba</code> is "the verified main game loop," correcting what it described as an error in an earlier version of this article that placed the loop in a symbol called <code>_main</code>. Both halves of that claim are addressed by the evidence above: this article has never referenced any symbol called <code>_main</code> at any point (there is nothing to correct), and the real decompiled <code>_escoba</code> — short, single-call-site, immediately delegating to a file-parsing utility — is not consistent with being the main loop. This is recorded in full in the [[#Cross-verification log|Cross-verification log]].
