|}

==== Symbols claimed by a secondary source: partial retraction ====

{{Note|'''This article previously stated, incorrectly, that the entire <code>emws_*</code> symbol set was absent from both binaries. That claim is retracted below with the full reasoning, rather than silently corrected — the error is instructive and is documented for that reason.}}

For completeness, the following symbol names were explicitly searched for in the boundary-safe extraction of both <code>HARE.EXE</code> and <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> and remain '''genuinely not found in either''': <code>_video</code>, <code>_DRV</code>, <code>_VOICE_DRV</code>, <code>_CTVDSK_DRV</code>, <code>_READ_DSP_TIME</code>, <code>_WRITE_DSP_TIME</code>, <code>_READ_DSP</code>, <code>_WRITE_DSP</code>, <code>_codificar</code>, <code>_juego</code>.

'''The <code>emws_*</code> set and <code>emuTop@</code>, by contrast, are genuinely present in both binaries — the earlier claim that they were absent was wrong, and the error is fully diagnosed below rather than merely reversed.''' The boundary-safe symbol scanner used throughout this article only begins collecting a candidate token when it encounters a literal underscore byte immediately following a non-identifier byte — a design that correctly isolates Borland's leading-underscore public-symbol convention (<code>_hare_x</code>, <code>_flags</code>, and the like), but silently skips any string that does '''not''' begin with an underscore, even if an underscore appears later in the same token. <code>emws_version</code> begins with the letter <code>e</code>, not an underscore; the scanner's boundary check at the embedded underscore (preceded by the identifier character <code>s</code> from "emws") correctly refuses to treat that position as a new token start, precisely per its own logic — the tool did exactly what it was written to do, and what it was written to do had an undocumented blind spot for exactly this shape of string. Direct string search (unconstrained by the token-boundary assumption) finds the complete set, unambiguously, in both files:

{| class="wikitable"
! File !! Offset !! Complete cluster found (in order, contiguous)
|-
| <code>HARE.EXE</code> || 0x13662–0x13712 || <code>emws_limitSP</code>, <code>emws_initialSP</code>, <code>emws_saveVector</code>, <code>emws_nmiVector</code>, <code>emws_status</code>, <code>emws_control</code>, <code>emws_TOS</code>, <code>emws_adjust</code>, <code>emws_fixSeg</code>, <code>emws_BPsafe</code>, <code>emws_stamp</code>, <code>emws_version</code>, <code>emuTop@</code>, <code>C0C</code>, <code>C0C</code>, <code>HARE.C</code>, <code>HARE</code>
|-
| <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> || 0x1290d–0x129be || byte-identical cluster, immediately followed by <code>C0C</code>, <code>C0C</code>, <code>SCOVA.C</code>, <code>SCOVA</code>
|}

'''This comparison is itself the correction's strongest evidence.''' The cluster is byte-for-byte identical in both executables, positioned identically relative to each binary's own base module name — despite <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> using LIM EMS 4.0 (confirmed via its exclusive <code>_ems_*</code> function set, unaffected by any of this) and <code>HARE.EXE</code> using no EMS calls whatsoever. A symbol cluster tied to the game's own EMS usage would be expected to '''differ''' between an EMS-using and a non-EMS-using build; an identical cluster in both is the signature of a generic, statically-linked runtime-library component, present because it was linked in regardless of whether the game calls it. The naming — a saved/initial stack pointer pair, a saved interrupt vector pair (ordinary and NMI), a status/control word pair, a "TOS" (top-of-stack), a segment-fixup field, a stack-frame safety flag, and a version stamp — reads far more coherently as '''Borland's 8087 floating-point emulator library''' performing emulated-FPU context save/restore across interrupts, a standard component of the Turbo C 2.0 runtime for systems without a hardware coprocessor, than as anything related to LIM EMS memory management. The "ems" in <code>emws</code> most likely abbreviates "emulator" in this context, not "Expanded Memory Specification" — a coincidental prefix collision that led both this article's earlier draft and at least one secondary source to the same wrong association.

The immediately adjacent <code>C0C</code> entries (appearing twice in each binary, right before the base module name) additionally confirm the exact Borland startup module used: '''<code>C0C.OBJ</code>, the Compact memory model''' startup file (small code, far/large data) — superseding this article's earlier, more hedged "medium/large model" language with a direct, source-confirmed answer.

==== Unresolved: the 7×16 byte table at 0xC630 ====

Immediately following the string cluster documented under [[#Embedded strings and file references|Embedded strings and file references]] sits a compact 7-row × 16-column byte table, with most cells holding <code>0xFF</code> and a scattering of small non-<code>0xFF</code> values (observed range 0–35 decimal). Two competing readings were considered:

* '''A dialogue/action index table''', keyed by some combination of room and object/interaction slot, with <code>0xFF</code> meaning "no action here."
* '''An unrelated palette or coordinate fragment''', given the isolated <code>B1 5F</code> ×3 repeat at its tail (see the save-format re-verification note above).

Neither reading has been confirmed. This table is '''not''' the save-format buffer that a secondary source associated with it (see the correction notes under [[#Save format — GAMESAVE, AUXILIO, AUXILIAR|Save format]]); its actual purpose remains open and would require disassembly of the code that indexes into it to resolve.

==== Original source module structure (confirmed from the TDS unit list) ====

Beyond the public symbol table, the TDS trailer also carries a '''unit/module list''' — the names of every source file (C and assembly) and every linked library module that contributed to the build. Extracting this list directly confirms the exact original source organization:

{| class="wikitable"
! Module !! Type !! Role
|-
| <code>HARE.C</code> || C source || Main game logic — the literal original filename, embedded in the binary's own debug info
|-
| <code>SONIDO</code> || C source || Sound module (Spanish: "sound") — a separate compilation unit from the main file
|-
| <code>MUSICA</code> || C source || Music module (Spanish: "music") — likewise separate
|-
| <code>SBCRWIO.ASM</code> || Assembly || Sound Blaster card read/write I/O
|-
| <code>VECTOR.ASM</code> || Assembly || Interrupt vector handling
|-
| <code>SCANINT.ASM</code> || Assembly || Almost certainly the keyboard-scancode dispatch routine independently confirmed by direct disassembly under [[#Cross-verification log|Cross-verification log]] (the 3-entry jump table at file offset 0x8C50) — this module list gives that confirmed mechanism its real source-file name
|-
| <code>VOCDATA.ASM</code> || Assembly || VOC (voice) data tables
|-
| <code>SBCDATA.ASM</code> || Assembly || Sound Blaster card data tables
|-
| <code>CTVDASM.ASM</code>, <code>CTVMEM.ASM</code>, <code>CTVDSK.ASM</code>, <code>CTVMASM.ASM</code> || Assembly || Creative Technology Voice Driver (CTVD) and Music (CTVM) low-level assembly interface — directly corresponding to the <code>_ctvd_*</code>/<code>_ctvm_*</code> API symbols already documented above
|}

The same unit list also confirms the exact compile-time include path <code>C:\TC\INCLUDE\SVGA256.H</code> — revealing that the original developers used a '''custom, non-stock VGA Mode 13h header''' (Turbo C 2.0 does not ship a file by this name), installed under the classic default <code>C:\TC</code> Turbo C installation directory. Everything else in the unit list (<code>FOPEN</code>, <code>STRCMP</code>, <code>LSEEK</code>, <code>ATEXIT</code>, and roughly forty more like them) are standard Borland Turbo C 2.0 CRT library module names, statically linked in — not part of the game's own source. The game's own original source, in its entirety, is therefore three C files and nine assembly files: a genuinely small, tightly-scoped codebase for what it accomplishes.

=== SCOVA.EXE ===

A compiled, EMS-dependent variant (77,863 bytes) sharing the same compiler lineage and 328 TDS symbols in common with <code>HARE.EXE</code> out of 347 total (boundary-safe count). Requires 256 KB LIM EMS 4.0. Not required to play the game; appears to be a development/testing build rather than the shipped executable.

Nineteen symbols are confirmed present '''only''' in <code>SCOVA.EXE</code>, all EMS-related, consistent with the LIM EMS 4.0 API already documented under [[#Memory model|Memory model]]:

{| class="wikitable"
! Symbol !! Role
|-
| <code>_ems_inst</code> / <code>_ems_version</code> || EMS driver presence check and version query (INT 67h AH=46h)
|-
| <code>_ems_alloc</code> / <code>_ems_free</code> || Allocate/free logical EMS pages (INT 67h AH=43h/45h)
|-
| <code>_ems_map</code> || Map a logical page into one of the four physical window slots (INT 67h AH=44h)
|-
| <code>_ems_frame_seg</code> || Query the page-frame segment address (INT 67h AH=41h)
|-
| <code>_ems_save_map</code> / <code>_ems_restore_map</code> || Preserve/restore the current page mapping context
|-
| <code>_ems_free_page</code> / <code>_ems_num_page</code> || Page-count bookkeeping
|-
| <code>_emm_ec</code> || Last EMM error code
|-
| <code>_falta_ems</code> || Fatal-error handler for "not enough EMS" conditions
|-
| <code>_handle</code> / <code>_handle2</code> || EMS handle storage (a second handle suggests two independent allocations, not a single 256 KB block)
|-
| <code>_intdos</code> || Generic <code>INT 21h</code> wrapper, listed here as it appears among the EMS-cluster symbols in the binary's layout though it is not EMS-specific itself
|}

=== SBFMDRV.COM ===

A 6,183-byte DOS TSR: '''Creative Sound Blaster FM-Driver, version 1.11''' (Creative Labs / Creative Technology, 1990), identification string <code>"FMDRV"</code> at offset 3. Drives the Yamaha OPL2 chip for CMF music playback, default I/O base 0x220, command-line switches <code>/P:</code> (port), <code>/I:</code> (IRQ), <code>/U</code> (uninstall). Must be resident before <code>HARE.EXE</code> is launched; for a ScummVM implementation this TSR is not needed at all, since ScummVM has its own software OPL2 emulation (<code>audio/fmopl.h</code>) that can consume CMF register data directly.

Byte-exact structure, independently confirmed:

{| class="wikitable"
! Offset !! Bytes !! Meaning
|-
| 0x0000 || <code>E9 D7 15</code> || <code>JMP near</code>, relative displacement 0x15D7, resolving to entry point '''0x15DA''' (confirmed: 3 + 0x15D7 = 0x15DA exactly)
|-
| 0x0003 || <code>"FMDRV"</code> + NUL || TSR identification string, used by the driver's own residency check to detect an already-installed copy
|-
| 0x11B8 || <code>"Creative Sound Blaster FM-Driver  Version 1.11\r\n"</code> || Version banner (confirmed at this exact offset)
|-
| 0x11E8 || <code>"Copyright (c) Creative Labs, Inc., 1990"</code> || Copyright banner, immediately following the version string (confirmed at this exact offset)
|}

=== PLAY.EXE / VPLAY.EXE ===

Separate Microsoft-C-toolchain utilities, unrelated to the Borland-built game logic. <code>PLAY.EXE</code> (37,739 bytes) is an IFF ANIM sequence player, likely used for cutscenes. <code>VPLAY.EXE</code> (20,893 bytes) is Creative Technology's standalone VOC player, version 1.50 — useful as an independent way to confirm <code>.ALS</code> audio content during testing.

=== Compiler-generated strings (not game text — do not translate) ===

For anyone using this article's dialogue and error catalogs as a localization source (see [[#Dialogue database|Dialogue database]]): the three strings below are emitted by the '''Borland Turbo C runtime itself''', not by the game's own code, and appear in effectively every program built with this toolchain. They should never be included in a translation pass — a translated build should keep these in their original English/compiler form, exactly as the genuine 1994 binary does, or replace them with ScummVM's own equivalent runtime error handling rather than translating them as if they were game dialogue.

{| class="wikitable"
! String !! Offset !! Origin
|-
| <code>Turbo-C - Copyright (c) 1988 Borland Intl.</code> || 0xBCA4 || Borland Turbo C 2.0 CRT identification banner
|-
| <code>Divide error</code> || 0xBCCF || Borland CRT's handler for CPU exception vector 0 (see the <code>__Int0Vector</code> discussion under [[#Game loop and timing|Game loop and timing]])
|-
| <code>Abnormal program termination</code> || 0xBCDD || Borland CRT's generic fatal-exit message
|}

<code>PLAY.EXE</code> and <code>VPLAY.EXE</code> carry the corresponding Microsoft-toolchain equivalent, confirmed at offset 0x84A4 in <code>PLAY.EXE</code>: <code>"MS Run-Time Library - Copyright (c) 1987, Microsoft Corp"</code> — again, compiler boilerplate, not game text.

== Development tools ==

Two distinct QuickBASIC 4.5 tools were used during the game's development, confirmed to be genuinely separate programs (not versions of one another) by direct comparison:

{| class="wikitable"
! Tool !! Size !! Routines !! Role
|-
| <code>SCOVA.ALC</code> (+ near-identical revision <code>SCOVA2.ALC</code>) || 391 / 367 lines || 9 <code>SUB</code>/<code>FUNCTION</code> blocks || Scene-layout editor; its <code>FUNCTION GRABAR</code> is the authoritative source for the <code>.ALD</code> format (see above). Displays a developer in-joke at startup referencing "Pendulo Estudios" (Péndulo Studios, a contemporary Spanish adventure-game house).
|-
| <code>CACA.ALC</code> || 1,001 lines || 31 <code>SUB</code>/<code>FUNCTION</code> blocks || A substantially larger, structurally distinct level-editing tool. Writes <code>FLAGS.DAT</code>, <code>MAPA.DAT</code>, <code>OBJETOS.DAT</code>, <code>PANT.DAT</code>, <code>VERBOS.DAT</code>, and <code>SALIDAS.DAT</code> — none of which correspond to the <code>GAMESAVE</code>/<code>AUXILIO</code>/<code>AUXILIAR</code> save-file naming (see save-format section above; this rules out <code>CACA.ALC</code> as the tool responsible for those files).
|}

Neither tool's source contains the literal strings <code>"auxilio"</code> or <code>"gamesave"</code>, which is the direct evidence behind the "open question" framing in the save-format section above.

=== CACA.ALC — complete routine index ===

All 31 top-level <code>SUB</code>/<code>FUNCTION</code> blocks, confirmed by direct extraction from the source file, grouped by apparent role:

{| class="wikitable"
! Group !! Routines
|-
| Top-level menu handlers (one per data domain) || <code>SUB BANDERAS</code>, <code>SUB MAPA</code>, <code>SUB OBJETOS</code>, <code>SUB PANTALLA</code>, <code>SUB VERBOS</code>, <code>SUB SALIR</code>
|-

This confirms <code>CACA.ALC</code> as a complete, self-contained CRUD editor for the five game data domains (flags, map/connectivity, objects, screens/backgrounds, verbs) plus a hardware-abstraction layer of its own (mouse and keyboard primitives distinct from the main game's own input handling) — a materially larger scope than <code>SCOVA.ALC</code>'s single-purpose <code>.ALD</code> scene editor.

{{Note|'''On an unsupported authorship attribution:''' a secondary analysis source attributed this codebase to a named individual, "Santiago Lancha," reasoning from the presence of hardcoded Spanish-language punctuation and phrasing. That reasoning does not support the conclusion it draws — Spanish punctuation is evidence of a Spanish-speaking developer or target audience, not of any specific person's identity — and the name does not appear anywhere in <code>HARE.EXE</code>, <code>SCOVA.EXE</code>, <code>SCOVA.ALC</code>, <code>SCOVA2.ALC</code>, <code>CACA.ALC</code>, or <code>SBFMDRV.COM</code> (checked directly, byte-for-byte, in all six files). This attribution is not repeated as fact anywhere else in this article and should not be treated as established.}}

{{Note|'''Internal inconsistency in a secondary source:''' the same analysis document states, in one section, that 218 Borland CRT functions are embedded in <code>HARE.EXE</code>, and in its own summary/conclusion section, that the figure is 77. The two numbers are not reconciled anywhere in that document. Given this internal contradiction, neither figure is repeated here as fact; readers wanting a CRT function count should rely on the boundary-safe total symbol count (348, see [[#Toolchain identification|Toolchain identification]]), which does not attempt to separate "CRT-library" symbols from "game-specific" ones.}}

== Puzzle flag state machine ==

The complete, currently-known puzzle graph, expressed as preconditions and effects on the flag set documented under [[#Save format — GAMESAVE, AUXILIO, AUXILIAR|Save format]]. This is the single most directly useful section of this article for reimplementing correct game '''logic''' (as opposed to correct file I/O) — a straightforward <code>switch</code>/<code>if</code> chain over these rows reproduces the entire known puzzle sequence.

{| class="wikitable"
! Step !! Precondition !! Trigger !! Effect
|-
| P01 || <code>door_open</code> == false || Click Scene 10 door object (→ Scene 9) || Fires DLG001 ("Sorry, I can't let you through."); no state change; navigation blocked
|-
| P02 || <code>switch_used</code> == false || Click Scene 10's interactive object (security switch) || Fires DLG003 ("It's a security door..."); sets <code>switch_used</code> = true
|-
| P03 || doors along Scenes 1→2→3→…→10→11 all otherwise passable || Walk the chain || Reach Scene 11 and encounter the large NPC hotspot ("Mariano")
|-
| P04 || <code>met_mariano</code> == false || Click the Scene 11 NPC hotspot, first time || Fires DLG007 + DLG008 (greeting, then "I'm sad... and hungry"); sets <code>met_mariano</code> = true
|-
| P05 || <code>got_food</code> == false || Click the disc-object sprite in Scene 2 or Scene 3 (the vending machine) || Fires DLG004 ("It's a human sausage vending machine."); sets <code>got_food</code> = true; adds a food item to inventory
|-
| P06 || <code>met_mariano</code> == true '''and''' inventory contains food || Click the Scene 11 NPC hotspot again || Fires DLG010 ("You keep the karma, read this book."); sets <code>gave_food</code> = true; removes food from inventory; adds a book item
|-
| P07 || inventory contains the book '''and''' <code>door_open</code> == false || Return to Scene 10, click the blocked door object again || Fires DLG013 (8.02 s, the longest line in the game — "You've proven yourself..."); sets <code>door_open</code> = true; Scene 9 becomes reachable
|-
| P08 || <code>door_open</code> == true || Walk through the now-unblocked door into Scene 9 || Scene 9 reached; from there the game continues '''backward''' through the Scene 7 hub to Scenes 8, 6, 5, and the 1–4 cluster — see the complete graph below
|}

{{Note|'''Correction: this puzzle sequence is not "linear and single-branch."''' An earlier revision of this article drew that conclusion honestly from the five scenes available at the time, which genuinely did form an unbranched chain. With the complete eleven-scene distribution obtained, Scenes 5 and 7 are confirmed junction rooms with three connections each (see the complete scene graph immediately below), meaning the explorable space is a branching graph, not a single corridor. The eight-step P01–P08 puzzle chain above remains accurate as the sequence of '''gating conditions''' — nothing about the flag logic itself changes — but it should not be read as implying the game's rooms form a straight line; Scenes 4, 6, 8 in particular are reachable at points along this chain without being strictly "on the path" P01–P08 describes, since the P01–P08 sequence tracks flag-gated progress, not room-by-room traversal order.}}

== Relationship to the existing Alcachofa engine ==

ScummVM already contains an engine internally named '''<code>alcachofa</code>''' (actively developed by Helco at the time of writing), targeting the early-2000s '''3D Mortadelo y Filemón''' titles for Windows. The name collision with this article's subject is coincidental — same studio, unrelated codebase and unrelated technology generation. Concretely, the existing engine is:

* An OpenGL/TinyGL 3D renderer with a camera and world-space scene graph.
* Driven by a real bytecode script virtual machine (a <code>ScriptOp</code> enum with 30-plus opcodes, procedures, and behaviors).
* Built around its own binary resource formats (<code>.nkr</code>, <code>.BIN</code>) with no relation to <code>.ALD</code>/<code>.ALG</code>/<code>.ALS</code>.
* Windows-native, not MS-DOS.

None of the existing engine's rendering, scripting, or resource-loading code is reusable for the 1994 DOS title documented on this page: there is no shared bytecode VM to target (this title has none at all), no shared 3D pipeline (this title is 2D Mode 13h), and no shared file formats. A completely separate engine module is required. If this article's subject proceeds to implementation, using a distinct internal engine name (proposed: <code>paco1994</code>) avoids any ambiguity with the unrelated OpenGL engine in source, detection tables, and this wiki's own category structure.

== ScummVM implementation ==

=== Detection ===

Minimum required files: <code>HARE.EXE</code> plus at least one matching <code>.ALD</code>/<code>.ALG</code> pair.

{| class="wikitable"
! File !! MD5 !! Size
|-
| HARE.EXE || <code>ed599780592c0302a571c88967e54b12</code> || 81,179
|-
| SCOVA.EXE || <code>d9c9f5aae31b5ee9beaeb8e9a492bf6c</code> || 77,863
|-
| PLAY.EXE || <code>7c0a32f587eaba83d41a4589e3bd7e7c</code> || 37,739
|-
| VPLAY.EXE || <code>b9301f9b7801693e202c9bffe544558d</code> || 20,893
|-
| SBFMDRV.COM || <code>382a4acdb8f3929a2c117826095f626e</code> || 6,183
|}

<syntaxhighlight lang="cpp">
{
    "pacohare1994",
    nullptr,
    AD_ENTRY1s("HARE.EXE", "ed599780592c0302a571c88967e54b12", 81179),
    Common::ES_ESP,
    Common::kPlatformDOS,
    ADGF_FREEWARE | ADGF_UNSTABLE,
    GUIO_NOSPEECH
},
</syntaxhighlight>

<code>ADGF_UNSTABLE</code> is correct for the engine's current "Not Yet Implemented" status; this becomes <code>ADGF_TESTING</code> only once the engine moves to "Added." The detection table above (matching the pattern in real ScummVM engines such as <code>engines/efh/detection.cpp</code>, verified directly against the public ScummVM source repository) is normally embedded directly in <code>detection.cpp</code> — a separate <code>detection_tables.h</code> is not the typical layout for a small single-game engine, and this article's draft C++ code should be reorganized to match before submission.

=== Build configuration ===

Verified directly against the ScummVM source repository (<code>engines/*/configure.engine</code> across several small, dependency-free engines): the build-registration file follows a fixed field order, <code>add_engine [name] [desc] [build-by-default] [subengines] [base games] [deps] [components]</code>, with trailing empty fields omittable. A minimal, dependency-free entry for this engine:

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
# engines/paco1994/configure.engine
add_engine paco1994 "Paco1994" no
</syntaxhighlight>

<code>no</code> for build-by-default matches the convention for a "Not Yet Implemented" engine; real examples in the current source (e.g. <code>engines/efh/configure.engine</code>) show that trailing empty-string fields for subengines/base-games/dependencies can simply be omitted rather than written out as explicit <code>""</code> — Paco1994 needs no special dependency (no 16-bit color, no PNG, no Bink) so the three-argument form above is sufficient. A matching minimal <code>module.mk</code>, following the same real-engine pattern:

<syntaxhighlight lang="make">
MODULE := engines/paco1994

MODULE_OBJS = \
	ald_parser.o \
	detection.o \
	game_state.o \
	interaction.o \
	paco1994.o

MODULE_DIRS += \
	engines/paco1994

ifeq ($(ENABLE_PACO1994), DYNAMIC_PLUGIN)
PLUGIN := 1
endif

include $(srcdir)/rules.mk
</syntaxhighlight>

=== Reusable ScummVM subsystems ===

No engine-specific code is reusable from the existing <code>alcachofa</code> engine (see previous section), but several general-purpose ScummVM subsystems require no modification at all:

{| class="wikitable"
! ScummVM subsystem !! Covers
|-
| <code>Image::PCXDecoder</code> (<code>image/pcx.h</code>) || <code>.ALG</code> backgrounds — standard PCX v3.0, no deviation found
|-
| <code>Audio::makeVOCStream</code> (<code>audio/decoders/voc.h</code>) || <code>.ALS</code> dialogue and SFX — standard VOC 1.10, no deviation found
|-
| <code>OPL::OPL</code> / OPL2 emulation (<code>audio/fmopl.h</code>) || CMF music playback, once a CMF sequencer is written to feed it (SBFMDRV.COM itself is not needed)
|}

What must be written from scratch: the <code>.ALD</code> parser (XOR-0xFF decode plus the field layout documented above, including the height-bug workaround), the hardcoded interaction/dialogue logic (there being no bytecode to interpret), the save-format reader/writer (pending resolution of the two open questions above), and the sprite compositor for <code>99.ALG</code> once that asset is located.

=== Implementation status ===

A prototype engine skeleton has been drafted following the "siloed logic" pattern — one small handler class per scene, rather than one monolithic switch statement, to keep the hardcoded per-scene logic testable and legible. Modules drafted so far: MZ/TDS static analysis tooling, an <code>.ALD</code> parser, a game-state/flag/inventory container, a per-scene interaction dispatcher, and a skeletal main engine class with the render-layer pipeline stubbed in. A parallel, fully working '''Python reference implementation''' (pygame-based, no C++ toolchain required to run it) exists and has been verified to correctly decode and render all five available scenes headlessly; it is intended purely as a behavioral reference for the eventual C++ port, not as a component to be shipped.

The three excerpts below are taken directly from the drafted (not pseudocode) C++ source, to make concrete exactly how the format specifications earlier in this article translate into engine code.

'''<code>AldParser::parseScene()</code> — the core parsing loop''' (full file: <code>ald_parser.cpp</code>), directly implementing the field layout from [[#.ALD — scene layout data|.ALD — scene layout data]] including the terminator check and the height-bug workaround noted there:

<syntaxhighlight lang="cpp">
// Step 4: Parse header fields
uint cursor = 0;
scene.sceneId   = lines[cursor++];      // Line 1: P$ — scene identifier
scene.musicFile = lines[cursor++];      // Line 2: MU$(0) — CMF filename
int16 nop = parseInt(lines[cursor++]);  // Line 3: NOP(0) — object count
int16 nod = parseInt(lines[cursor++]);  // Line 4: NOD(0) — disc-object count

// Step 5: Parse NOP on-screen objects (hotspots and doors)
scene.objects.clear();
for (int16 i = 0; i < nop; i++) {
    AldObject obj;
    obj.id   = parseInt(lines[cursor++]);  // NUM(I)
    int16 x1 = parseInt(lines[cursor++]);  // X1(I)
    int16 y1 = parseInt(lines[cursor++]);  // Y1(I)
    int16 x2 = parseInt(lines[cursor++]);  // x2(I)
    int16 y2 = parseInt(lines[cursor++]);  // y2(I)
    obj.rect = Common::Rect(x1, y1, x2 + 1, y2 + 1); // ScummVM rects are half-open

    int16 isDoor = parseInt(lines[cursor++]); // PUER(I): 0=object, 1=door
    obj.isDoor = (isDoor != 0);

    if (obj.isDoor) {
        obj.destScene  = lines[cursor++];           // e.g. "5.ALD"
        obj.destDoorId = parseInt(lines[cursor++]); // PDN(I)
        obj.destPos    = parseInt(lines[cursor++]); // PPOS(I): 0=left,1=right,2=center
    }
    scene.objects.push_back(obj);
}

// Step 6: Validate terminator "99"
if (cursor >= (uint)lines.size() || lines[cursor] != "99") {
    warning("AldParser: Expected terminator '99' at line %u, got '%s'",
            cursor, cursor < (uint)lines.size() ? lines[cursor].c_str() : "<EOF>");
    return false;
}
cursor++; // consume "99"

// Step 7: Parse NOD disc-object sprites
// IMPORTANT: sheetRect.bottom = sheetRect.top + 39 (BUGGY in GRABAR).
// Actual sprite height = 24px. Use AldDiscObject::kTrueHeight, NOT sheetRect.height().
scene.discObjects.clear();
// ... (mirrors the object loop above; see #99.ALG for the height-bug detail)
</syntaxhighlight>

'''<code>InteractionDispatcher::dispatchClick()</code> — the complete hotspot hit-test''' (full file: <code>interaction.cpp</code>), the direct C++ equivalent of the reconstructed <code>_comprueba(x,y)</code> pseudocode under [[#Reconstructed control flow (pseudocode)|Reconstructed control flow]]:

<syntaxhighlight lang="cpp">
bool InteractionDispatcher::dispatchClick(int16 x, int16 y,
                                          const AldScene &scene,
                                          GameState &state,
                                          Paco1994Engine &eng) {
    if (!_handler) {
        warning("InteractionDispatcher: no handler for scene '%s'", _sceneId.c_str());
        return false;
    }

    // Hit-test all ALD on-screen objects in order (matches original _comprueba loop)
    // First match wins — objects are listed in ALD order from GRABAR.
    for (uint i = 0; i < scene.objects.size(); i++) {
        const AldObject &obj = scene.objects[i];

        // Rect::contains() checks x1<=x<x2, y1<=y<y2 (half-open interval)
        if (!obj.rect.contains(x, y))
            continue;

        if (obj.isDoor)
            _handler->handleDoor(obj, state, eng);
        else
            _handler->handleObject(obj.id, state, eng);

        return true; // hotspot hit
    }

    // No hotspot hit: Paco walks to click position (_lleva_al_hare)
    return false;
}
</syntaxhighlight>

'''Per-scene handler dispatch''' (full file: <code>interaction.h</code>/<code>.cpp</code>) — the "siloed logic" pattern itself, one small class per scene rather than one large <code>switch</code>, directly implementing the [[#Puzzle flag state machine|Puzzle flag state machine]] table above for Scene 10 (the security switch and the blocked door):

<syntaxhighlight lang="cpp">
void Scene10Handler::handleObject(int16 objId, GameState &state, Paco1994Engine &eng) {
    if (objId == 40) {                          // security switch (P02)
        if (!state.getFlag(kFlagSwitchUsed)) {
            fireDialogue(kDlgSecurityDoor, state, eng);   // sets kFlagSwitchUsed
        } else {
            eng.showDialogue("The switch has already been activated.", "");
        }
    }
}

void Scene10Handler::handleDoor(const AldObject &obj, GameState &state, Paco1994Engine &eng) {
    if (obj.id == 39) {                         // blocked door to Scene 9 (P01/P07)
        if (state.getFlag(kFlagDoorOpen)) {
            eng.transitionToScene(obj.destScene, obj.destDoorId, obj.destPos);
        } else if (state.hasItem(kItemBook) && state.getFlag(kFlagReadBook)) {
            fireDialogue(kDlgGuardPass1, state, eng);     // sets kFlagDoorOpen (P07)
        } else {
            fireDialogue(kDlgBlockedDoor, state, eng);    // P01
        }
    } else if (obj.id == 41) {
        eng.transitionToScene(obj.destScene, obj.destDoorId, obj.destPos); // always passable
    }
}
</syntaxhighlight>

These three excerpts, together with the reference decoders under [[#File formats|File formats]] and the masked-blit/page-flip implementations under [[#Rendering pipeline|Rendering pipeline]], cover every piece of engine logic needed to reproduce the five available scenes' complete behavior in a from-scratch reimplementation.

== Modding and community completion ==

Because the spatial layer is fully data-driven, new or replacement scenes are mechanically straightforward to author once the format above is implemented: paint a 320×200 256-color PCX background, write a plain-text scene descriptor in the layout above and XOR-0xFF it, and record any dialogue as 21,739 Hz 8-bit unsigned mono VOC. Filling in the six missing scenes (4 through 9) to complete the game's narrative arc is technically approachable this way, but constitutes a derivative work and should be pursued only alongside the rights-clearance effort described in [[#Legal status|Legal status]] above, not ahead of it.

With scenes 4–9, the sprite sheet, the voice driver, and all five music files now obtained, a ScummVM reimplementation has access to essentially the complete original asset set. The one substantive remaining gap — Paco's own on-screen sprite — is now a precisely-scoped extraction task (search inside <code>HARE.EXE</code>) rather than an open-ended search for a missing external file.

== Cross-verification log ==

This article has absorbed material from more than one independent analysis pass, including at least one secondary source that mixed genuine findings with unverified or incorrect additions. In the interest of not silently propagating the incorrect portions — and of not silently discarding the substantial genuinely-useful portions either — every specific, falsifiable claim contributed by that pass was individually checked against the actual binaries before being either incorporated or excluded. This table is the complete record of that check.

{| class="wikitable"
! Claim !! Verdict !! Evidence
|-
| Boundary-safe TDS symbol count is ~398 || '''Revised to 348/347''' || Naive substring scanning inflates the count by slicing tokens mid-identifier; a boundary-safe re-extraction (token must start immediately after a non-identifier byte) gives 348 (<code>HARE.EXE</code>) / 347 (<code>SCOVA.EXE</code>), closer to an earlier 351 estimate than to 398
|-
| ~55 specific new symbol names across video, sprite, character, mouse, sound, and slot-machine subsystems || '''Confirmed''' || Individually checked present in the boundary-safe symbol set; incorporated throughout [[#HARE.EXE|HARE.EXE]]
|-
| <code>emws_*</code> EMS-manager symbol set (13 names) claimed present || '''This article's own initial verdict was wrong — retracted''' || Initially reported as absent due to a blind spot in this article's own boundary-safe scanner (see the full diagnosis under [[#Symbols claimed by a secondary source: partial retraction|HARE.EXE]]). The cluster is genuinely present, byte-identical, in both binaries — but the evidence points to a generic statically-linked 8087 floating-point emulation library component, not game-specific EMS-management code as originally guessed by this article and by the secondary source alike.
|-
| <code>__Int0Vector</code>/<code>__Int4Vector</code> constitute an INT 08h/INT 1Ch timer hook || '''Symbols confirmed, interpretation corrected''' || The symbols exist but index Borland CRT CPU-exception vectors (INT 0/4/5/6 decimal — divide error, overflow, etc.), not BIOS/DOS timer interrupts; see [[#Game loop and timing|Game loop and timing]]
|-
| SBFMDRV.COM entry point, identification string, and version/copyright string offsets || '''Confirmed exactly''' || <code>JMP</code> target 0x15DA, <code>"FMDRV"</code> at 0x0003, version string at 0x11B8, copyright string at 0x11E8 — all byte-exact matches; see [[#SBFMDRV.COM|SBFMDRV.COM]]
|-
| 24 embedded asset filenames with specific offsets || '''Confirmed exactly''' || All 24 found at the claimed offsets; see [[#Embedded strings and file references|Embedded strings and file references]]
|-
| 7 additional error-message strings with specific offsets || '''Confirmed exactly''' || All 7 found at the claimed offsets; incorporated
|-
| 104-byte "save buffer" embedded in <code>HARE.EXE</code> at 0xC628–0xC68F, with specific marker bytes at offsets 0x62 (<code>0x0F</code>) and 0x65 (<code>0x23</code>) || '''Rejected''' || Real bytes at those offsets are <code>0xB1</code> and <code>0x5F</code>; the range also starts inside a run of null padding with no structural boundary marker; see [[#Save format — GAMESAVE, AUXILIO, AUXILIAR|Save format]]
|-
| Save routine opens a file named <code>"auxilio"</code>, writes 104 bytes, applies <code>_codifica</code> (XOR-0xFF) || '''Contradicted by direct evidence''' || Real sample files <code>GAMESAVE</code>/<code>AUXILIO</code>/<code>AUXILIAR</code> are 100% plain ASCII text with no XOR transform; see [[#Save format — GAMESAVE, AUXILIO, AUXILIAR|Save format]]
|-
| Eight (later extended to seventeen) specific disassembly addresses (0x8775–0x8C65) are <code>CALL</code>/<code>JMP</code> instructions in the main loop || '''This article's own earlier verdict was wrong — now fully confirmed''' || The original "not confirmed" verdict resulted from '''this article's own incorrect offset-mapping assumption''' (adding the 512-byte header size to the logical address before locating it in the file). Re-tested using the correct convention (file offset = logical address directly, no header addition): all 17 claimed addresses resolve to the claimed opcode (<code>0x9A</code> FAR CALL or <code>0xE8</code> NEAR CALL), '''and''' every NEAR CALL's relative displacement, computed independently, lands exactly on the claimed target address — 17/17 confirmed, including the full jump-target chain. This is a correction to this article's own prior skepticism, not merely a secondary source's claim being accepted. See [[#Reconstructed control flow (pseudocode)|Reconstructed control flow]].
|-
| A "continuation-passing" 3-entry jump dispatcher at 0x8C52–0x8CA1, described as popping a return address, advancing it past the CALL opcode, and jumping through it || '''Confirmed, with one notation correction''' || The exact byte sequence is present at file offset 0x8C50 (2 bytes from the claimed 0x8C52, a labeling/counting difference rather than a content error). One imprecision: the claim's assembly notation writes the final jump as <code>JMP [CX]</code> (memory-indirect through the address stored at the location CX points to) — but <code>CX</code> is not a valid base/index register in 16-bit x86 real-mode addressing, so no disassembler can produce that operand form. The actual byte found (<code>FF E1</code>) is <code>JMP CX</code> (register-indirect: jump to the address held directly in CX), a different and perfectly valid encoding. The underlying discovery is correct; only the prose transcription of the addressing mode was imprecise.
|-
| This 3-entry jump dispatcher, and a related ASCII-scancode-to-index mapping routine, constitute "a small bytecode interpreter" comparable to Sierra SCI/AGI or LucasArts SCUMM || '''Mechanism confirmed; the framing is not adopted''' || The underlying jump-table/keyboard-shortcut mechanism is real (see above) and is a normal, mundane compiler/hand-optimization pattern for dispatching a small fixed set of keyboard shortcuts — not a general-purpose bytecode virtual machine driving game logic. This article does not adopt the Sierra SCI/AGI/SCUMM comparison: those engines interpret externally-stored bytecode for arbitrary puzzle/dialogue logic, which this game's puzzle and dialogue logic (confirmed extensively elsewhere in this article) does not have — it remains hardcoded C. A local jump-table for keyboard shortcuts does not change the [[#Overview|hybrid data-driven/hardcoded architecture]] finding at the top of this article.
|-
| CT-VOICE.DRV entry point and identification string at specific offsets || '''Now confirmed''' || Originally logged as unverifiable (file unavailable). Since obtained from the complete distribution: entry point is a <code>JMP near</code> to exactly 0x0754, with the <code>"CT-VOICE"</code> string confirmed at offset 0x0003 — both match the original claim exactly

| Codebase attributed to a named individual, "Santiago Lancha" || '''Rejected''' || Name does not appear in any of six examined binaries/sources; the reasoning offered (Spanish-language strings) does not support identifying a specific person
|-
| 218 vs. 77 Borland CRT functions embedded || '''Internal contradiction in the source, not adjudicated''' || The secondary source states both figures in different sections without reconciling them; neither is repeated here as fact
|-
| Reconstructed initialization sequence, game loop, and hotspot-dispatch pseudocode || '''Plausible, consistent with verified symbols, presented as reconstruction''' || Matches the confirmed symbol table and existing puzzle-tree documentation; incorporated as illustrative pseudocode, not as a disassembly transcript

Direct inspection resolved this rather than assuming either the best or worst case: <code>HARE.EXE</code>'s real symbols (<code>_num_room</code>, <code>_hare_x</code>, <code>_escoba</code>, etc.) are confirmed absent from <code>PLAY.EXE</code>'s actual decompilation, so the file-identity mixing is real -- but the underlying "segment 0x0810" value is not itself invented: Reko genuinely labels <code>VPLAY.EXE</code>'s code with that segment number (946 occurrences confirmed directly), a labeling convention this article's own faster first pass initially and wrongly dismissed as fabricated by checking only Ghidra's different numbering. * <code>_escoba</code> is "the verified main game loop" -- '''confirmed, on the second, more careful pass'''. This article's own first attempt to check this claim read only the loop's exit condition, not its full body, and wrongly reported the claim as refuted; a subsequent, independently-sourced document prompted a re-check that read the complete loop body and reversed that verdict -- see the full, corrected account under [[#HARE.EXE|HARE.EXE]]. The companion claim that this corrects an alleged prior reference to a symbol called <code>_main</code> remains unsupported: this article has never referenced any such symbol.

=== Provenance note: the MiniMax family ===

A family of six secondary analysis documents examined across this article's research (titled variously <code>BINARY_ARCHAEOLOGY_FINAL</code>, <code>BYTECODE_DISPATCHER</code>, <code>COMPARATIVA_FINAL</code>, <code>PACO_HARE_1994_RE_ENGINE</code>, <code>PACO_HARE_1994_MASTER</code>, plus the already-covered <code>AUXILIO_format_analysis</code> and <code>HARE_EXE_CATALOGO_COMPLETO</code>) self-identifies its own authorship, in the master document, as "MiniMax," a separate AI system, dated July 2026.

A consistent pattern emerges across the set: genuinely correct, independently-verifiable technical detail (the CT-VOICE.DRV and SBFMDRV.COM byte offsets, and the confirmed 17-address jump dispatcher — see [[#Reconstructed control flow (pseudocode)|Reconstructed control flow]]) sits alongside recurring fabrication and, in one case, an error that turned out to be this article's own rather than the source's:

* '''Fabrication:''' "Santiago Lancha" as an author, searched for as an exact literal string per <code>PACO_HARE_1994_MASTER</code>'s own specific claim, and confirmed absent from every binary and source file examined.
* '''This article's own error, since corrected:''' the <code>emws_*</code> symbol set, which multiple documents in this family correctly reported as present, was incorrectly marked absent in an earlier revision of this article due to a blind spot in its own verification tooling — see [[#Symbols claimed by a secondary source: partial retraction|the full diagnosis]].
* '''Independently disproven factual errors:''' VOC version claimed as 1.20 (real value: 1.10); a systematic mislabeling of the real SS:SP header pair as CS:IP, appearing identically in two different documents in the set, for both <code>HARE.EXE</code> and <code>SCOVA.EXE</code> separately.
* '''A repeated internal-arithmetic tell:''' three separate instances of a document's own supporting category breakdown failing to sum to its headline total — 347 vs. a claimed 398 for a symbol count, 16 vs. a claimed 17 for a CALL count, 131 vs. a claimed 130 for a verification-check count.
* '''Fabricated content baked into compiled code:''' the family's accompanying <code>alcachofa_engine/</code> C source bakes several of these errors into constants (<code>PACO_SPRITE_W 40</code> against a directly-verified real value of 39; <code>PACO_VRAM_SIZE 65536</code> against a real, exact 64,000; swapped sample-rate labels for voice vs. sound-effect VOCs), and additionally invents gameplay features with no basis anywhere in the actual game (a named companion character, cloud save, achievements, cooperative multiplayer).

None of this invalidates the set's genuinely correct portions, several of which are credited by name at their respective points in this article — but nothing from this family is taken on trust without the same direct byte-level check applied to every other source here.

=== Provenance note: PACO_EXE_Analisis_Forense ===

A separate document, <code>PACO_EXE_Analisis_Forense</code>, analyzes a binary it calls <code>PACO.EXE</code> at approximately 134,224 bytes. Every core numeric claim in it (file size, MZ header fields, relocation count) fails to match the real <code>HARE.EXE</code> examined throughout this article.

However, its own internal "verified evidence" table honestly attributes the 134,224-byte figure to "user specification," not to independent measurement. That figure and filename match, exactly, the hypothetical starting premise given at the very beginning of this article's own research process, before any real game files had been supplied — strongly suggesting this document was produced by a parallel process working from that same initial, later-superseded premise, without ever receiving the real files this article's own analysis is built on, rather than fabricating a false measurement.

Treated fairly on that basis: its foundational binary-structure claims (MZ header, memory map, interrupt vector table) do not describe the real file and are not incorporated, but several of its higher-level conclusions — reached from a genuinely different, much smaller evidence base (10 sample assets, by its own account) — are directionally correct and independently corroborate this article's own findings:

* <code>.ALD</code> files are XOR-0xFF encrypted plaintext (confirmed).
* The existing ScummVM <code>alcachofa</code> engine is architecturally incompatible, using a different asset format and its own bytecode VM for unrelated, later titles (confirmed, matching this article's own [[#Relationship to the existing Alcachofa engine|analysis]]).

Its claimed VOC version, 1.20, is wrong (the real value, confirmed repeatedly throughout this article, is 1.10) — notably the '''same specific error''' made independently by <code>PACO_HARE_1994_MASTER</code> from the unrelated MiniMax family, a curious point of convergence rather than evidence either copied the other.
